```{r}
#| include: false
# Load ggplot2 for the consistently formatted rendered figures in this chapter.
library(ggplot2)
```

# Introduction

In this chapter, we learn how to estimate the parameters of a model and their uncertainty
by maximum likelihood. In [Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd) we estimated parameters with
the method of moments, which only uses the mean and the variance of a sample. Maximum
likelihood uses the probability that the model assigns to every observation, and it applies
to any model for which we can write a probability mass or density function. This is why it
is the method of estimation in the rest of the course. The concepts of Chapter 3
(estimator, sampling distribution, standard error and confidence interval) remain the same;
we now apply them to a different estimator.

The chapter has two parts. The first builds the method: the likelihood function, maximum
likelihood estimation with `optim()` and the package RTMB, and models with several
parameters. The second is about what we can say once a model is fitted: the uncertainty of
the estimates, the properties of maximum likelihood estimators and the comparison of models
with information criteria. Two examples run through the chapter. The first is the counts of
balsam fir seedlings in 50 quadrats of Chapter 3, under a Poisson model, of which we also use
the first ten quadrats where the shape of the likelihood matters. The second is the number of
calls made by barn owl nestlings, the field data of the Chapter 3 practical, under a
Negative Binomial model with two parameters.

# Learning goals

In this chapter, we will cover:

- the likelihood function and the log-likelihood;
- maximum likelihood estimation by numerical optimisation;
- constraints on parameters and transformations;
- likelihood surfaces, slices and profiles for models with several parameters;
- standard errors from the curvature of the log-likelihood, and Wald intervals;
- likelihood profile intervals and joint confidence regions;
- the properties of maximum likelihood estimators in large and small samples;
- the comparison of models with the Akaike information criterion.

We will use the [Poisson](../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-poisson) and
[Negative Binomial](../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-negative_binomial) distributions
throughout the chapter. They are described in the
[Supplement](../Supplements/distributions.qmd). We write and fit the models with the
packages RTMB and RTMBdist, whose distribution functions we have used since Chapter 2.

The table below is a roadmap of the chapter. Each row is one step, with the question that
it answers, the R tools that we use for it and the example on which we show it.

| Step | Question it answers | In R | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Part 1** | | | |
| The likelihood | How probable are the data for a given value of the parameter? | `dpois(..., log = TRUE)`, `sum()` | Fir seedlings |
| Estimation | Which value of the parameter makes the data most probable? | NLL with `getAll()`, `cmb()`, `MakeADFun()`, `optim()` | Fir seedlings |
| Transformations | How do we keep a parameter within its range? | `exp()`, `plogis()` | Fir seedlings |
| Several parameters | What does the likelihood look like, and what does it say about one parameter? | `dnbinom2()`, `for` loops with `obj$fn()`, `contour()` | Owls |
| **Part 2** | | | |
| Standard errors | How precise is the estimate? | `sdreport()` and `ADREPORT()` | Fir seedlings and owls |
| Confidence intervals | Which parameter values do the data support? | Wald interval on the fitted scale; profile with `TMB::tmbprofile()` and `confint()` | Fir seedlings and owls |
| Properties | Why does the method work, and when does it fail? | Simulation with `obj$simulate()` | Owls |
| Model comparison | Which of two models is better supported by the data? | AIC | Owls |

# The likelihood function {#sec-likelihood}

The **likelihood function** is the joint probability of the observed sample, read as a
function of the parameters of the model with the data held fixed. For continuous data it is
the joint density of the sample. Let $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ be the observations and assume that
they are i.i.d. with a distribution that has a parameter $\theta$ (as in Chapter 3,
$\theta$ stands for a parameter in general). The likelihood of $\theta$ is

$$
L(\theta\mid x_1,\ldots,x_n)
= P(X_1=x_1,\ldots,X_n=x_n\mid\theta)
= \prod_{i=1}^{n}P(X_i=x_i\mid\theta),
$$

where $P(X_i=x_i\mid\theta)$ is the probability mass that the model assigns to the
observation $x_i$ when the parameter is $\theta$,^[The vertical bar reads "for a given
value of": $P(X=x\mid\theta)$ is the probability of $x$ for a given value of $\theta$, and
$L(\theta\mid x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ is the likelihood of $\theta$ for a given sample. The same
symbol is used for conditional distributions, which are introduced in
[Chapter 7](../Chapter_7/Theory.qmd#sec-conditional).] and the symbol $\prod$ denotes a product over the
$n$ observations, in the same way as $\sum$ denotes a sum. The second equality holds
because the observations are independent, so their joint probability is the product of
their individual probabilities (see
[Chapter 2](../Chapter_2/Theory.qmd#sec-joint-independence), where we announced that the
i.i.d. assumption would be fundamental for estimation). For continuous data we replace each
probability mass by the density $f_X(x_i\mid\theta)$.

This is the formula of a joint distribution from Chapter 2. What changes is what we hold
fixed. In Chapter 2 we fixed the parameters and calculated the probability of different
possible samples. Now the sample has been observed, so $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ are fixed numbers,
and we look at how the probability of that sample changes as we vary $\theta$. A parameter
value under which the observed sample is more probable is better supported by the data;
that is the crucial idea behind likelihood.^[Fisher introduced the maximum likelihood method
in 1912, in a paper that he wrote as an undergraduate student and in which he called it an
"absolute criterion". He introduced the word likelihood in 1921, to keep this quantity apart
from a probability, and the name "maximum likelihood" in 1922, in the paper that set out the
theory of the method. Choosing the parameter value under which the observations are most
probable had been anticipated in the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries by Lambert,
Daniel Bernoulli and Gauss, although without a reasoned defence of the method. If you want
to read more about this history, see Aldrich (1997), "R. A. Fisher and the making of
maximum likelihood 1912–1922", *Statistical Science* 12: 162–176, and Stigler (2007), "The
epic story of maximum likelihood", *Statistical Science* 22: 598–620.] The likelihood is
the basis of everything that follows in this book: the estimates, their confidence
intervals and the comparison of models are all calculated from it.

Let's illustrate it with the counts of balsam fir seedlings in 50 quadrats of
[Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd#sec-estimates), where $X_i$ is the number of seedlings
in quadrat $i$ and $X_i \sim \operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda)$. The probability mass
function of the Poisson distribution is
$P(X_i=x_i\mid\lambda)=e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{x_i}/x_i!$. We start with a case that is small
enough to do by hand, the counts of the first three quadrats (0, 1 and 2). Their
likelihood is the product of three contributions (remember that $0!=1$):

$$
L(\lambda\mid 0,1,2)
= \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{0}}{0!}\times
  \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{1}}{1!}\times
  \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{2}}{2!}
= \frac{e^{-3\lambda}\lambda^{3}}{2}.
$$

For $\lambda=1$ this gives $e^{-3}/2\approx 0.0249$ and for $\lambda=2$ it gives
$e^{-6}\,2^{3}/2\approx 0.0099$.

To verify our maths with R, we first load the packages RTMB and RTMBdist and the counts of
the 50 quadrats, as in Chapter 3:

```{r}
#| message: false
# Load RTMB first and RTMBdist second.
library(RTMB)
library(RTMBdist)

# Counts of balsam fir seedlings in 50 quadrats (see ?boot::fir), as in Chapter 3,
# and the number of quadrats.
data(fir, package = "boot")
seedling_counts = fir$count
n_quadrats = length(seedling_counts)
```

`dpois()` returns the contribution of each of the three counts for a given value of
$\lambda$, and `prod()` multiplies them:

```{r}
# The counts of the first three quadrats.
first_counts = seedling_counts[1:3]
first_counts

# Probability of each of the three counts at lambda = 1.
dpois(x = first_counts, lambda = 1)

# Likelihood of the three counts: prod() multiplies their probabilities.
prod(dpois(x = first_counts, lambda = 1))
prod(dpois(x = first_counts, lambda = 2))
```

The two products are the values that we calculated by hand. These three counts are about 2.5
times more probable under a mean of 1 than under a mean of 2 (their own mean is 1). The
likelihood of the whole sample is calculated in the same way:

```{r}
# Likelihood of all 50 counts at lambda = 1 and at lambda = 2.
prod(dpois(x = seedling_counts, lambda = 1))
prod(dpois(x = seedling_counts, lambda = 2))
```

With the 50 counts the order is reversed: the whole sample is about $3\times10^{10}$ times
more probable under a mean of 2 than under a mean of 1, so 50 quadrats discriminate between
these two values far more strongly than three. Note how small both numbers are. Every
observation multiplies the likelihood by a probability smaller than one, so **its value
depends on the number of observations and has no meaning by itself**. What we use is the
comparison between the likelihoods of different parameter values for the same data.

A likelihood is calculated from probabilities but it is not a probability distribution for
the parameter, for two reasons:

1. We work with aleatoric probability ([Chapter 2](../Chapter_2/Theory.qmd)): probabilities
   describe how the data or estimates vary across hypothetical samples, while the parameter
   of the model is a fixed quantity.^[The likelihood is also at the core of Bayesian
   inference. There it is multiplied by a prior distribution, which describes what is known
   about the parameter before seeing the data, and the product is rescaled to give a
   probability distribution for the parameter (the posterior distribution).
   [Chapter 1](../Chapter_1/Theory.qmd) explains why this book stays with the Frequentist
   interpretation.] So in the model there is no variation or error about $\lambda$ to which
   a probability could refer.

2. For a fixed $\lambda$ the probabilities of all the possible samples add up to one, but
   nothing forces the likelihoods of all the possible values of $\lambda$ to do so for a
   fixed sample. For the 50 counts, the area under the likelihood across all the possible
   values of $\lambda$ is approximately $8.7\times10^{-40}$, which is very far from one.

```{r}
#| include: false
# Closed-form Poisson likelihood of a sample of counts. Unlike a product of dpois() over
# the data, this function accepts a vector of lambda values, which integrate() needs.
# It is calculated on the log scale and then exponentiated, because lambda^sum(counts)
# is too large for the computer at the large values of lambda that integrate() tries.
poisson_likelihood = function(lambda, counts) {
  exp(-length(counts) * lambda + sum(counts) * log(lambda) - sum(lfactorial(counts)))
}

# Area under the likelihood across all possible values of lambda. The likelihood is
# tiny, so the default absolute tolerance is too coarse: we set it to zero and ask
# for a small relative error instead.
integrate(
  f = poisson_likelihood,
  lower = 0,
  upper = Inf,
  counts = seedling_counts,
  rel.tol = 1e-8,
  abs.tol = 0
)
```

::: {.callout-warning title="A likelihood is not the probability of a parameter value"}
The likelihood $L(\theta\mid x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ is the probability (or density) of the
observed data for a given value of the parameter, read as a function of the parameter. It
does not tell us how probable a parameter value is. We use it to compare parameter values:
the data are better supported by the value with the higher likelihood.
:::

## The log-likelihood

With a larger sample the product of probabilities can become smaller than the smallest
positive number that the computer can represent, and R then returns zero. For this reason,
and because sums are easier to work with than products, we use the **log-likelihood**, the
natural logarithm of the likelihood:

$$
\ell(\theta\mid x_1,\ldots,x_n)
= \log\left(L(\theta\mid x_1,\ldots,x_n)\right)
= \sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\left(P(X_i=x_i\mid\theta)\right).
$$

The logarithm turns the product into a sum. It is an increasing function, so a parameter
value with a higher likelihood also has a higher log-likelihood, and both functions have
their maximum at the same value of $\theta$. Once the data are fixed we will write
$L(\theta)$ and $\ell(\theta)$ for short.

In R, all the `d*` functions have an argument `log`. With `log = TRUE` they return the
logarithm of the probability mass (or density), which is more accurate than calculating
the probability first and taking its logarithm afterwards. The log-likelihood is the sum
of these values. To see where the product fails, we simulate 1,000 counts from a Poisson
model with $\lambda=4$:

```{r}
# Likelihood and log-likelihood of a large simulated sample of 1,000 counts at lambda = 4.
set.seed(seed = 501)
many_counts = rpois(n = 1000, lambda = 4)

# The product is smaller than the smallest positive number R can represent.
prod(dpois(x = many_counts, lambda = 4))

# The sum of log probabilities is an ordinary number.
sum(dpois(x = many_counts, lambda = 4, log = TRUE))
```

R returns zero for the product, although none of the probabilities in it is zero, whereas
the log-likelihood is an ordinary number. From here on we always work with
log-likelihoods.

For continuous data the contributions to the likelihood are densities. Recall from
[Chapter 2](../Chapter_2/Theory.qmd#sec-continuous_measurements) that a density has units
(one over the unit of the measurement), that it changes with those units and that it can
be larger than one. The log-likelihood inherits these properties: **it can be positive**,
and **its value changes if we express the same measurements in other units**. For example,
if body masses are converted from grams to kilograms, the density of every mass is
multiplied by 1,000 (the same probability is spread over a thousand times fewer units), so
the log-likelihood of $n$ masses increases by $n\log(1000)$. This shift is a constant, so
the differences between the log-likelihoods of two parameter values, or of two models, are
the same in both units. In general, the value of a log-likelihood means nothing by itself,
and only differences between log-likelihoods calculated from the same data are meaningful.

:::: {#imp-crab-burrows .callout-important title="crab burrows"}

Three plots on a mudflat contain 3, 1 and 2 crab burrows. Assume that the counts are i.i.d.
with a Poisson distribution. On paper, write the likelihood as a function of $\lambda$ and
calculate the likelihood and the log-likelihood for $\lambda=2$ and for $\lambda=3$ burrows
per plot. Which of the two values is better supported by the data?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

The likelihood is the product of the three contributions:

$$
L(\lambda\mid 3,1,2)
= \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{3}}{3!}\times
  \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{1}}{1!}\times
  \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{2}}{2!}
= \frac{e^{-3\lambda}\lambda^{6}}{12}.
$$

For $\lambda=2$ the likelihood is $64e^{-6}/12\approx 0.0132$ and the log-likelihood is
$-6+\log(64/12)\approx -4.33$. For $\lambda=3$ the likelihood is $729e^{-9}/12\approx 0.0075$
and the log-likelihood is $-9+\log(729/12)\approx -4.89$. The data are better supported by
$\lambda=2$, which is the mean of the three counts. The difference between the two
log-likelihoods is 0.57, so the counts are about 1.8 times more probable ($e^{0.57}$)
under $\lambda=2$ than under $\lambda=3$. In R:

```{r}
# Log-likelihood of the three counts at lambda = 2 and at lambda = 3.
burrow_counts = c(3, 1, 2)
sum(dpois(x = burrow_counts, lambda = 2, log = TRUE))
sum(dpois(x = burrow_counts, lambda = 3, log = TRUE))
```

:::
::::

# Maximum likelihood estimation {#sec-maximum-likelihood}

The **maximum likelihood estimator** (MLE) of a parameter is the value of the parameter for
which the likelihood of the observed sample is highest:

$$
\hat\theta
= \underset{\theta}{\arg\max}\;L(\theta\mid x_1,\ldots,x_n)
= \underset{\theta}{\arg\max}\;\ell(\theta\mid x_1,\ldots,x_n),
$$

where $\arg\max$ reads "the value of $\theta$ at which the function reaches its maximum".
That is, $\max$ would give the height of the highest point and $\arg\max$ gives its
location. In plain English, the MLE is the parameter value under which the model assigns
the highest probability to the data that we observed. As we saw in
[Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd#sec-estimates), the procedure of calculation is called
estimator and the value that it returns for a given sample is the estimate; we use the
abbreviation MLE for both.

At the highest point of the log-likelihood its slope is zero (if you need to refresh how
a derivative is calculated, see the
[rules of differentiation](../Supplements/calculus.qmd#sec-calc-rules) of the calculus
refresher). For i.i.d. Poisson counts, setting the derivative of the log-likelihood with
respect to $\lambda$ to zero and solving for $\lambda$ gives

$$
\hat\lambda=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i=\overline x.
$$

So the MLE of $\lambda$ is the mean of the sample, which is also the method-of-moments
estimator of [Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd#sec-estimates), and for the 50 counts it
is 2.14 seedlings per quadrat:

```{r}
# The maximum likelihood estimate of the Poisson mean is the mean of the counts.
lambda_hat = mean(seedling_counts)
lambda_hat
```

A solution that can be written as a formula, like this one, is called a **closed-form**
solution, and it exists only for a few models.^[The Normal model is another of them. The
MLE of $\mu$ is the mean of the sample and the MLE of $\sigma^2$ is the variance with
divisor $n$, that is, the method-of-moments estimators of
[Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd#sec-two_parameters). The MLE of the variance is
therefore biased.] For the others, setting the derivatives to zero gives equations that
cannot be solved with algebra, and we find the maximum numerically, with an algorithm that
searches for it. That is the method that we use in the rest of the book, because it works
for any model for which we can write a likelihood.

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true" icon=false title="Statistical detail: deriving the Poisson estimator"}
At the maximum of a smooth curve
the slope is zero, so we differentiate the log-likelihood with respect to the parameter,
set the derivative to zero and solve for the parameter. For i.i.d. Poisson counts:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ell(\lambda)
&= \sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\left(\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{x_i}}{x_i!}\right)
= -n\lambda+\log(\lambda)\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log(x_i!),\\
\frac{d\ell}{d\lambda}
&= -n+\frac{1}{\lambda}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i,\\
0 &= -n+\frac{1}{\hat\lambda}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\hat\lambda=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i=\overline x.
\end{aligned}
$$

The last term of the log-likelihood does not contain $\lambda$, so it disappears when we
differentiate.^[The derivative of the log-likelihood with respect to a parameter is called
the **score**. The MLE is the value of the parameter(s) at which the score is zero.] The second
derivative, $-\sum x_i/\lambda^2$, is negative, which confirms that the point where the
slope is zero is a maximum (derivatives, and what they tell us about the shape of a
function, return in [Chapter 5](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd)). In R:

```{r}
# The derivative of the log-likelihood, sum(x) / lambda - n, is zero at that value.
sum(seedling_counts) / lambda_hat - n_quadrats
```
:::

## The likelihood curve

A **likelihood curve** is the log-likelihood of a model with one parameter, drawn as a
function of that parameter. It shows where the maximum is and how quickly the
log-likelihood falls on either side of it, which is what we will use in
@sec-likelihood-uncertainty to calculate confidence intervals. We plot it as a **relative
log-likelihood**, which is the difference between the log-likelihood and its maximum,

$$
\ell(\theta)-\ell(\hat\theta),
$$

so that the curve is zero at the estimate and negative everywhere else. We draw all the
likelihood figures of this chapter on this scale, because only differences in
log-likelihood are meaningful.

The shape of a likelihood curve is easier to see in a small sample, so from here on we use
the first ten quadrats for the curve and for the uncertainty of $\lambda$. They contain 22
seedlings, so their estimate is 2.2 seedlings per quadrat:

```{r}
# The counts of the first ten quadrats and their maximum likelihood estimate.
ten_counts = seedling_counts[1:10]
lambda_hat_ten = mean(ten_counts)
lambda_hat_ten
```

To draw the curve, we define a grid of values of $\lambda$ and fill a vector with the
log-likelihood at each of them, using a `for` loop:

```{r}
# Candidate values of lambda (seedlings per quadrat).
lambda_grid = seq(from = 0.8, to = 5, by = 0.05)

# Pre-allocate a vector for the log-likelihood and fill it with a loop over the grid.
loglik_grid = rep(NA, times = length(lambda_grid))
for (i in seq_along(lambda_grid)) {
  loglik_grid[i] = sum(dpois(x = ten_counts, lambda = lambda_grid[i], log = TRUE))
}
```

We then subtract the log-likelihood at the estimate from every value of the grid. We also
calculate the relative log-likelihood at two values of $\lambda$ that are one seedling
away from the estimate, on either side of it:

```{r}
# Relative log-likelihood: the difference from the log-likelihood at the estimate.
loglik_lambda_hat_ten = sum(dpois(x = ten_counts, lambda = lambda_hat_ten, log = TRUE))
relative_loglik = loglik_grid - loglik_lambda_hat_ten

# Relative log-likelihood at 1.2 and at 3.2 seedlings per quadrat.
sum(dpois(x = ten_counts, lambda = 1.2, log = TRUE)) - loglik_lambda_hat_ten
sum(dpois(x = ten_counts, lambda = 3.2, log = TRUE)) - loglik_lambda_hat_ten
```

The curve reaches its maximum at $\hat\lambda=2.2$ seedlings per quadrat
(@fig-likelihood_curve). Note that the curve is not symmetric: it falls more steeply to
the left of the maximum than to the right. The relative log-likelihood is $-3.33$ at
$\lambda=1.2$ and $-1.76$ at $\lambda=3.2$, so a mean of 3.2 is better supported by these
data than a mean of 1.2, although both are one seedling away from the estimate. This
asymmetry matters for confidence intervals (@sec-likelihood-uncertainty).

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-likelihood_curve
#| fig-cap: "Relative log-likelihood of the counts of fir seedlings in the first ten quadrats under a Poisson model, as a function of the mean number of seedlings per quadrat. The vertical line marks the maximum."
# Plot the relative log-likelihood curve and mark its maximum.
curve_data = data.frame(lambda = lambda_grid, relative = relative_loglik)
ggplot(curve_data, aes(x = lambda, y = relative)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = lambda_hat_ten,
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "grey40"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-8, 0)) +
  labs(
    x = expression(paste("Mean seedlings per quadrat, ", lambda)),
    y = "Relative log-likelihood"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

A grid of values shows us the curve. To find its highest point for any model, with any
number of parameters, we use an optimiser.

## Numerical optimisation

An **optimiser** is an algorithm that searches for the parameter values at which a function
reaches its minimum. It starts from values that we provide, evaluates the function, and
moves step by step towards lower values until it cannot improve any further. In R we use
the function `optim()`. Since it minimises, we do not give it the log-likelihood but the
**negative log-likelihood** (NLL), $-\ell(\theta)$: the parameter value with the lowest NLL
is the one with the highest likelihood.

In this book every NLL is written in the same form, which the package RTMB needs. It is a
function with two arguments, both of them named lists: the first holds the parameters
(`parms`) and the second the data (`data`). Its first line calls `getAll()`, which makes
the elements of both lists available by their names, so that the rest of the function
reads like the model. For the Poisson model the list of parameters has one element,
`lambda`, and the list of data has one element, `counts`:

```{r}
# Negative log-likelihood of Poisson counts. The first argument holds the parameters
# and the second the data, both as named lists.
poisson_nll_lambda = function(parms, data) {
  # Make the elements of both lists available by name.
  getAll(parms, data)
  -sum(dpois(x = counts, lambda = lambda, log = TRUE))
}
```

Three steps take us from this function to the estimate. First, we connect the likelihood
to a data set with a small helper function, `cmb()`, which takes an NLL and a list of data
and returns the NLL of those data as a function of the parameters only. This way we can
later calculate the same likelihood on other data, as long as the variables in the list
have the same names.

```{r}
# Connect a likelihood to a data set.
cmb = function(f, d) function(p) f(p, d)
```

Second, `MakeADFun()` processes the NLL so that the tools that we use
in the rest of the course can work with it (the details are explained progressively
through the course). We give it the function returned by `cmb()` and a list with the
starting value of every parameter, and it returns the object that the optimiser needs:

```{r}
# Process the NLL of the 50 counts, with a starting value of 1 seedling per quadrat.
# silent = TRUE stops MakeADFun() from printing its progress.
fir_lambda_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(poisson_nll_lambda, list(counts = seedling_counts)),
  list(lambda = 1),
  silent = TRUE
)
```

We take three elements from this object that are passed to the `optim()` function:

- `par`, the starting values as a vector;
- `fn`, the NLL as a function of that vector;
- and `gr`, the gradients of the NLL with respect to parameters (details on why we need it
  in [Chapter 6](../Chapter_6/Theory.qmd) and [Chapter 8](../Chapter_8/Theory.qmd#sec-gradients)).

```{r}
# optim() minimises fn, starting from par and using the slope gr.
fir_lambda_fit = optim(
  par = fir_lambda_obj$par,
  fn = fir_lambda_obj$fn,
  gr = fir_lambda_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
```

The fourth argument (`method`) determines which specific algorithm is used for optimisation.
We will use `"BFGS"` in most cases as it is quite efficient. `optim()` returns a list and
its most relevant elements are

- `par`, the value of the parameter at the minimum (i.e., the maximum likelihood estimate);
- `value`, the value of NLL at the maximum likelihood estimate;
- `convergence`, a code that is zero when the algorithm stopped normally, which is the
  first thing to check after every fit. If you get a value different from 0 that means
  something went wrong.

```{r}
# Estimate, minimum of the negative log-likelihood, and convergence code (0 = normal stop).
fir_lambda_fit$par
fir_lambda_fit$value
fir_lambda_fit$convergence
```

## Constraints and transformations {#sec-constraints}

A **constraint** is a restriction on the values that a parameter can take. The mean
$\lambda$ of a Poisson distribution must be positive, and a probability must lie between
zero and one. An optimiser such as BFGS does not know about these restrictions. It can try
any real number, and for a negative $\lambda$ the function `dpois()` returns `NaN` (not a
number). In the fit above the search stayed among positive values, but that is not
guaranteed. In this book we deal with constraints by **transforming** the parameter: the
optimiser works with a quantity that can take any real value, and the NLL function
converts it into the parameter of the model.

For a positive parameter we use the logarithm. The optimiser searches over
$\log(\lambda)$, which can be any real number, and inside the function `exp()` turns it
into a positive mean:

```{r}
# Negative log-likelihood on the log scale: log_lambda can take any real value
# and exp() turns it into a positive mean.
poisson_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  # Transform the parameter to the original scale.
  lambda = exp(log_lambda)
  -sum(dpois(x = counts, lambda = lambda, log = TRUE))
}
```

The steps of the fit are the same as before, with `log_lambda` in the list of starting
values. The element `par` of the fit is now the estimate of $\log(\lambda)$, which we
transform back with `exp()` to report it in seedlings per quadrat (`unname()` drops the
name `log_lambda`, which no longer describes the value):

```{r}
# Process the NLL of the 50 counts, starting from log(1), and fit it.
fir_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(poisson_nll, list(counts = seedling_counts)),
  list(log_lambda = log(1)),
  silent = TRUE
)
fir_fit = optim(par = fir_obj$par, fn = fir_obj$fn, gr = fir_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
fir_fit$convergence

# Estimate in seedlings per quadrat.
lambda_mle = unname(exp(fir_fit$par))
lambda_mle
```

The same NLL can be connected to another data set, as long as its list uses the same
name, `counts`. For the first ten quadrats, which we use again in
@sec-likelihood-uncertainty, only the list of data changes:

```{r}
# The same likelihood connected to the counts of the first ten quadrats.
fir_ten_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(poisson_nll, list(counts = ten_counts)),
  list(log_lambda = log(1)),
  silent = TRUE
)
fir_ten_fit = optim(
  par = fir_ten_obj$par,
  fn = fir_ten_obj$fn,
  gr = fir_ten_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
fir_ten_fit$convergence
```

For a probability $p$ the corresponding transformation is the **logit**,
$\operatorname{logit}(p)=\log\left(p/(1-p)\right)$, which covers all the real numbers as
$p$ goes from zero to one. In R, `qlogis()` calculates the logit and `plogis()` its
inverse, which turns any real number into a value between zero and one (the names come
from the logistic distribution, of which they are the quantile and cumulative probability
functions):

```{r}
# The logit transformation for a probability, and its inverse.
qlogis(p = 0.25)
plogis(q = qlogis(p = 0.25))
```

Fitting on a transformed scale and reporting on the original scale relies on a property of
maximum likelihood called **invariance**: the MLE of a function of a parameter is that
function of the MLE.^[See Zehna (1966), "Invariance of maximum likelihood estimators",
*Annals of Mathematical Statistics* 37: 744, for the general statement.] That is, for a
function $g$ of the parameter,

$$
\widehat{g(\theta)}=g(\hat\theta).
$$

Here the optimiser found the MLE of $\log(\lambda)$, and invariance tells us that its
exponential is the MLE of $\lambda$. The reason is that the transformation only relabels
the horizontal axis of the likelihood curve. Every value of $\log(\lambda)$ corresponds to
one value of $\lambda$ with the same likelihood, so the highest point is the same on both
scales.

Invariance also gives us the MLE of other quantities that are calculated from the
parameter. For example, under the Poisson model the probability that a quadrat has no
seedlings is $P(X=0\mid\lambda)=e^{-\lambda}$, and its MLE is
$e^{-\hat\lambda}\approx 0.12$. Note that invariance carries over the estimate but not
unbiasedness: [Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd#sec-sampling_distribution) showed that
$\hat\lambda$ is an unbiased estimator of $\lambda$, whereas $e^{-\hat\lambda}$ is a biased
estimator of $e^{-\lambda}$.

::: {.callout-note title="When a fit fails"}
Check the element `convergence` after every fit. A code other than zero means that the
search did not finish normally, and the values in `par` are then not estimates.

While it searches, `optim()` can try parameter values for which the NLL cannot be
calculated, and `fn` then returns `NaN` without a warning. BFGS treats such a value as a
failed step and tries a shorter one, so this is harmless when the search ends with
convergence code 0 and the estimates are sensible. When the NLL is `NaN` at the starting
values, `optim()` stops with the error "initial value in 'vmmin' is not finite".

If a fit fails, check first that every constrained parameter is transformed inside the
NLL. Then try other starting values (the method-of-moments estimates are a good choice),
look at the data, and calculate the NLL at the starting values, for example with
`fir_obj$fn(fir_obj$par)`, to see whether it returns an ordinary number.
[Chapter 8](../Chapter_8/Theory.qmd#sec-wrong-place) explains why optimisers fail and what else can be
done.
:::

:::: {#imp-ecological-scale .callout-important title="back to the ecological scale"}

A colleague fits two models with `optim()`. In the first, the parameter is the logarithm of
the mean number of ticks per lizard and the result is `par = 0.92`. In the second, the
parameter is the logit of the probability that a seed germinates and the result is
`par = -0.85`. Report both estimates on the ecological scale. Are they the maximum
likelihood estimates of the mean and of the probability?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

We apply the inverse of each transformation:

```{r}
# Inverse of the logarithm and inverse of the logit.
exp(0.92)
plogis(q = -0.85)
```

The estimates are approximately 2.5 ticks per lizard and a germination probability of
0.30. By invariance, they are the maximum likelihood estimates of the mean and of the
probability, because the optimiser found the maximum likelihood estimates of their
logarithm and logit.

:::
::::

# Models with several parameters {#sec-likelihood-surface}

With several parameters the likelihood is a function of all of them jointly, and the MLE is
the combination of values with the highest likelihood. The definitions of the previous
sections do not change, but the likelihood is now a surface over the parameters instead of
a curve. This raises two questions that did not exist with one parameter: how the estimates
of the different parameters depend on each other, and how to describe what the data say
about one of them. These questions matter for the rest of the book, because the models of
Chapters 6 and 7 always have several parameters.

We will use the barn owl data of the Chapter 3 practical to illustrate these concepts. The
data set `Owls` in the package `glmmTMB` contains observations of barn owl nests (Roulin
and Bersier 2007). For each visit of a parent to a nest, the variable `SiblingNegotiation`
is the number of calls made by the nestlings. As in that practical, we keep the visits of
the female parent to nests where the nestlings had been fed (`Satiated`), so that all
counts can reasonably share one mean. We also calculate the method-of-moments estimates of
the Negative Binomial model introduced below, which we will use as starting values:

```{r}
# Load the Owls data from the glmmTMB package without attaching the package.
data(Owls, package = "glmmTMB")

# Keep the visits of the female parent to nests with satiated nestlings.
satiated_female = Owls[Owls$FoodTreatment == "Satiated" & Owls$SexParent == "Female", ]

# Number of calls at each of these visits, and the number of visits.
call_counts = satiated_female$SiblingNegotiation
n_visits = length(call_counts)

# Method-of-moments estimates, as in the practical of Chapter 3.
mu_mom = mean(call_counts)
var_mom = mean((call_counts - mu_mom)^2)
k_mom = mu_mom^2 / (var_mom - mu_mom)

c(n_visits = n_visits, mu_mom = mu_mom, var_mom = var_mom, k_mom = k_mom)
```

There are 122 visits, with a mean of 4.75 calls per visit and a variance of 42.3, almost
nine times the mean. Let $X_i$ be the number of calls at visit $i$. Because of this
overdispersion we use a
[Negative Binomial](../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-negative_binomial) model with mean
$\mu$ and shape $k$,

$$
X_i \sim \operatorname{NegBin}(\mu, k), \qquad \operatorname{Var}(X_i)=\mu+\frac{\mu^2}{k},
$$

and we assume that the visits are i.i.d. (a simplification, because visits to the same
nest may resemble each other; models for such data are the subject of
[Chapter 7](../Chapter_7/Theory.qmd), whose practical fits a model with nests to these
visits). The method of moments gives
$\hat\mu=\overline x\approx 4.75$ calls per visit and $\hat k\approx 0.60$.

The NLL is written as before. The list of parameters now has two elements, `log_mu` and
`log_k` (both parameters are positive, so we use the logarithm for both), and the list of
data has one, `calls`. For the probability mass we use `dnbinom2()` of the package
RTMBdist, which is written in terms of the mean (`mu`) and the shape (`size`):

```{r}
# Negative log-likelihood of the Negative Binomial model with mean mu and shape k.
nb_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  # Transform the parameters to the original scale.
  mu = exp(log_mu)
  k = exp(log_k)
  -sum(dnbinom2(x = calls, mu = mu, size = k, log = TRUE))
}
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Two functions called `dnbinom2()`"}
The packages RTMB and RTMBdist both have a function called `dnbinom2()`, with different
arguments: in RTMBdist they are the mean and the shape (`mu` and `size`), and in RTMB the
mean and the variance (`mu` and `var`). R uses the function of the package that was
attached last, which is RTMBdist when we load `library(RTMB)` first and
`library(RTMBdist)` second, as at the start of this chapter. So always load both packages
in that order and name the arguments `mu` and `size`. If only RTMB is loaded, R stops
with an error about an unused argument `size`.
:::

The optimiser needs a starting value for each parameter. The method-of-moments estimates
are a sensible choice: they are quick to calculate and, being estimates of the same
parameters, they should not be far from the maximum. We give them to `MakeADFun()` in a
list with the names that the NLL uses, and `optim()` keeps those names in its result, so
we can select each estimate by its name and transform it back:

```{r}
# Process the NLL of the owl counts, starting from the method-of-moments estimates
# on the log scale.
owl_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(nb_nll, list(calls = call_counts)),
  list(log_mu = log(mu_mom), log_k = log(k_mom)),
  silent = TRUE
)

# Fit the model and check the convergence code.
owl_fit = optim(par = owl_obj$par, fn = owl_obj$fn, gr = owl_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
owl_fit$convergence

# Maximum likelihood estimates on the original scale.
mu_mle = unname(exp(owl_fit$par["log_mu"]))
k_mle = unname(exp(owl_fit$par["log_k"]))
c(mu_mle = mu_mle, k_mle = k_mle)
```

The estimate of the mean is the mean of the sample, 4.75 calls per visit: for a Negative
Binomial model the MLE of the mean is the mean of the sample, whatever the value of $k$.
The estimate of the shape is $\hat k\approx 0.33$, far from the method-of-moments estimate
of 0.60 at which the search started. The two methods are different estimators, so they give
different estimates from the same sample; we compare their precision in
@sec-mle_properties.

## The fitted model

`optim()` returns estimates for any model that we give it, so after a fit we check whether
the fitted model describes the data. For counts we can compare the relative frequency of
each count in the sample with the probability that the fitted model assigns to it
(@fig-owl_fits). As a reference we add a Poisson model with the same mean, its MLE. The
Negative Binomial model reproduces the high frequency of visits without calls (54 of the
122) and spreads the rest of its probability over a wide range of counts, whereas the
Poisson model concentrates its probability around the mean and makes a visit without calls
very rare. We compare the two models with a formal criterion in @sec-aic.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-owl_fits
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-cap: "Relative frequencies of the number of calls per visit (bars) and probabilities under the fitted models: Negative Binomial with maximum likelihood estimates, and Poisson with the sample mean."
# Relative frequencies of each count in the sample.
count_values = 0:max(call_counts)
observed_data = data.frame(
  count = count_values,
  frequency = tabulate(call_counts + 1, nbins = length(count_values)) / n_visits
)

# Fitted probabilities for each model at every possible count.
fitted_data = rbind(
  data.frame(
    count = count_values,
    probability = dnbinom2(x = count_values, mu = mu_mle, size = k_mle),
    model = "Negative Binomial (maximum likelihood)"
  ),
  data.frame(
    count = count_values,
    probability = dpois(x = count_values, lambda = mu_mom),
    model = "Poisson"
  )
)

# Bars for the sample and lines with points for the models.
ggplot() +
  geom_col(
    data = observed_data,
    aes(x = count, y = frequency),
    fill = "grey90",
    colour = "grey40"
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = fitted_data,
    aes(x = count, y = probability, colour = model, linetype = model),
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = fitted_data,
    aes(x = count, y = probability, colour = model, shape = model)
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c("#D55E00", "grey20")
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Number of calls per visit",
    y = "Relative frequency or probability",
    colour = NULL,
    linetype = NULL,
    shape = NULL
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "top", legend.direction = "vertical")
```

## The likelihood surface

With two parameters we can still evaluate the log-likelihood on a grid, which now has two
dimensions: one for the values of $\mu$ and one for the values of $k$. We store the results
in a matrix with one row per value of $\mu$ and one column per value of $k$, and fill it
with two nested `for` loops. Inside the loops we call `owl_obj$fn()`, which returns the
NLL for a vector of parameters on the scale that was optimised. So we give it the
logarithms of the candidate values and change the sign of the result. The maximum
log-likelihood is minus the element `value` of the fit:

```{r}
# Grids of candidate values for the mean (calls per visit) and the shape.
mu_grid = seq(from = 2.5, to = 9, length.out = 91)
k_grid = seq(from = 0.12, to = 0.75, length.out = 91)

# Pre-allocate a matrix and fill it with two nested loops: row i for the i-th mean
# and column j for the j-th shape. fn() takes log(mu) and log(k) and returns the NLL.
loglik_surface = matrix(NA, nrow = length(mu_grid), ncol = length(k_grid))
for (i in seq_along(mu_grid)) {
  for (j in seq_along(k_grid)) {
    loglik_surface[i, j] = -owl_obj$fn(c(log(mu_grid[i]), log(k_grid[j])))
  }
}

# Relative log-likelihood: the difference from the maximum found by optim().
loglik_nb = -owl_fit$value
relative_surface = loglik_surface - loglik_nb
```

A matrix like this one can be drawn with `contour()`, as we did in the Chapter 1 practical:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# The matrix can be drawn with contour(), as in the practical of Chapter 1.
contour(x = mu_grid, y = k_grid, z = relative_surface, levels = c(-6, -4, -3, -2, -1))
```

@fig-likelihood_surface shows the same contours. Each line joins the combinations of $\mu$
and $k$ that have the same relative log-likelihood, like the contours of the joint density
in [Chapter 2](../Chapter_2/Theory.qmd#sec-two_continuous_variables), and the MLE is at the
top of the hill. The contours are not tilted, because the best value of $\mu$ is the mean
of the sample for every value of $k$. They are not symmetric either: the surface falls more
slowly towards large values of $\mu$ and of $k$ than towards small ones.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-likelihood_surface
#| fig-cap: "Contours of the relative log-likelihood of the owl data as a function of the mean and the shape of the Negative Binomial model. The circle is the maximum likelihood estimate."
# Arrange the matrix as a data frame: mu varies fastest, as in as.vector() of the matrix.
surface_data = expand.grid(mu = mu_grid, k = k_grid)
surface_data$relative = as.vector(relative_surface)

# Contours of the relative log-likelihood with the maximum likelihood estimate.
ggplot() +
  geom_contour(
    data = surface_data,
    aes(x = mu, y = k, z = relative),
    breaks = c(-12, -9, -6, -4, -3, -2, -1),
    colour = "grey40"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = data.frame(mu = mu_mle, k = k_mle),
    aes(x = mu, y = k),
    colour = "#D55E00",
    size = 3
  ) +
  labs(
    x = expression(paste("Mean number of calls per visit, ", mu)),
    y = expression(paste("Shape, ", italic(k)))
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

## Parameterisation, slices and profiles {#sec-slices-profiles}

The same model can be written with different sets of parameters, each of which is called a
**parameterisation**. By invariance, the maximum and the fitted model are the same in every
parameterisation, but the shape of the surface around the maximum is not. The Negative
Binomial distribution, for example, can also be written with the shape $k$ and a
probability $p=k/(k+\mu)$, which are the arguments `size` and `prob` of `dnbinom()` (see
the [supplement entry](../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-nb-prob)). With this
parameterisation the contours of the owl surface are tilted (left panel of
@fig-slice_profile): a larger $k$ goes with a larger $p$, because the two together
determine the mean, which the data pin down well. Tilted contours describe estimates that
depend on each other. Whether they are tilted depends on the model, its parameterisation
and the data, so it cannot be generalised from one example. This book writes distributions
in terms of their mean where possible, because the models of later chapters describe how
the mean changes with covariates (see
[Parameterisations](../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-parameterisations) in the
supplement);
the choice of parameters also matters for numerical optimisation, which is a topic of
[Chapter 8](../Chapter_8/Theory.qmd#sec-scaling).

```{r}
#| include: false
# The owl model with the shape k (size) and probability p (prob) of dnbinom(), with log(k)
# and logit(p) as the transformed parameters.
nb_prob_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  k = exp(log_k)
  p = plogis(logit_p)
  -sum(dnbinom(x = calls, size = k, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}
owl_prob_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(nb_prob_nll, list(calls = call_counts)),
  list(log_k = log(k_mom), logit_p = qlogis(k_mom / (k_mom + mu_mom))),
  silent = TRUE
)
owl_prob_fit = optim(
  par = owl_prob_obj$par,
  fn = owl_prob_obj$fn,
  gr = owl_prob_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
owl_prob_fit$convergence

# Same maximum and same k as the first fit; p equals k / (k + mu) by invariance.
k_mle_prob = unname(exp(owl_prob_fit$par["log_k"]))
p_mle = unname(plogis(owl_prob_fit$par["logit_p"]))
c(k_mle_prob = k_mle_prob, p_mle = p_mle, loglik = -owl_prob_fit$value)
k_mle / (k_mle + mu_mle)

# Surface in k and p.
k_grid_prob = seq(from = 0.12, to = 0.75, length.out = 91)
p_grid = seq(from = 0.02, to = 0.16, length.out = 91)
loglik_surface_prob = matrix(NA, nrow = length(k_grid_prob), ncol = length(p_grid))
for (i in seq_along(k_grid_prob)) {
  for (j in seq_along(p_grid)) {
    loglik_surface_prob[i, j] =
      -owl_prob_obj$fn(c(log(k_grid_prob[i]), qlogis(p_grid[j])))
  }
}
surface_prob_data = expand.grid(k = k_grid_prob, p = p_grid)
surface_prob_data$relative = as.vector(loglik_surface_prob - loglik_nb)

# Slice: p is fixed at its estimate.
k_fine = seq(from = 0.12, to = 0.75, length.out = 127)
slice_loglik = rep(NA, times = length(k_fine))
for (i in seq_along(k_fine)) {
  slice_loglik[i] = -owl_prob_obj$fn(c(log(k_fine[i]), qlogis(p_mle)))
}

# Profile: tmbprofile() re-estimates p for each k. ytol = 10 continues it to 10 units
# below the maximum, beyond the lower limit of the figure.
owl_prob_profile_k = TMB::tmbprofile(owl_prob_obj, name = "log_k", ytol = 10, trace = FALSE)
profile_data = data.frame(
  k = exp(owl_prob_profile_k$log_k),
  relative = -owl_prob_profile_k$value - loglik_nb
)

# Path of the profile: for every k the MLE of the mean is the mean of the counts, so the
# best p is k / (k + mu_mle).
profile_data$p = profile_data$k / (profile_data$k + mu_mle)
```

A surface can only be drawn for two parameters, and even then we usually want to know what
the data say about one parameter at a time. There are two ways of reducing a likelihood
surface to a curve for one parameter, and they answer different questions. Let $\theta_1$
be the parameter of interest and $\theta_2$ the other parameter (or parameters). A
**likelihood slice** fixes the other parameters at their estimates and varies the parameter
of interest, $\ell(\theta_1,\hat\theta_2)$: it is a cut through the surface along a
straight line. A **likelihood profile** re-estimates the other parameters for every value
of the parameter of interest:

$$
\ell_{\mathrm{prof}}(\theta_1)=\max_{\theta_2}\,\ell(\theta_1,\theta_2).
$$

That is, for each value of $\theta_1$ we find the value of $\theta_2$ that maximises the
log-likelihood with $\theta_1$ held fixed, and we record that maximum. Which parameter we
profile depends on the question.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-slice_profile
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-cap: "Slice and profile of the log-likelihood for the shape k of the Negative Binomial model fitted to the owl data, in the parameterisation with k and p. Left: contours of the relative log-likelihood with the slice (dashed line) and the values of p that maximise the log-likelihood for each k (solid line). Right: relative log-likelihood along the slice and along the profile."
library(patchwork)

# Left panel: contours with the slice and the path of the profile.
left_panel = ggplot() +
  geom_contour(
    data = surface_prob_data,
    aes(x = k, y = p, z = relative),
    breaks = c(-12, -9, -6, -4, -3, -2, -1),
    colour = "grey40"
  ) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = p_mle, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#D55E00") +
  geom_line(data = profile_data, aes(x = k, y = p), colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(
    data = data.frame(k = k_mle_prob, p = p_mle),
    aes(x = k, y = p),
    colour = "#D55E00",
    size = 3
  ) +
  labs(
    x = expression(paste("Shape, ", italic(k))),
    y = expression(paste("Probability, ", italic(p)))
  ) +
  theme_classic()

# Right panel: relative log-likelihood along the slice and along the profile.
slice_profile_data = rbind(
  data.frame(k = k_fine, relative = slice_loglik - loglik_nb, curve = "Slice"),
  data.frame(k = profile_data$k, relative = profile_data$relative, curve = "Profile")
)
right_panel = ggplot(slice_profile_data, aes(x = k, y = relative, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-6, 0)) +
  labs(
    x = expression(paste("Shape, ", italic(k))),
    y = "Relative log-likelihood",
    linetype = NULL
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

left_panel | right_panel
```

@fig-slice_profile shows the slice and the profile of $k$ in the parameterisation with $k$
and $p$. The slice follows the horizontal line at $\hat p$, which leaves the high part of
the surface quickly because the contours are tilted. The profile follows the ridge of the
surface: for each $k$ it moves to the best $p$. Both pass through the MLE, and everywhere
else the profile is higher than the slice, since it is the maximum over all the values of
$p$. The slice is therefore narrower. It describes what the data would say about $k$ if we
knew $p$ exactly, whereas the profile takes into account that $p$ is estimated from the
same data. The profile does not depend on how the other parameters are written, whereas a
slice does: with $\mu$ and $k$, where the contours are not tilted, the slice and the
profile of $k$ coincide.

We will use profiles to calculate confidence intervals (@sec-profile_intervals), where a
function of TMB re-estimates the other parameters for us. Slices need no optimisation, so
they are a quick way to inspect a fitted model, and they return as a diagnostic in
[Chapter 8](../Chapter_8/Theory.qmd#sec-diagnosis).

::: {.callout-note title="Explore a likelihood surface"}
Kristoffer Magnusson's
[interactive page on maximum likelihood](https://rpsychologist.com/likelihood/) lets you
do by hand what an optimiser does. It uses a Normal model with two parameters, a mean and a
variance, and a sample of ten observations. In the part "Likelihood Calculation", move the
sliders of the mean and the variance and watch how the contribution of each observation
and the log-likelihood change. In "Finding the Maximum Likelihood Estimates", follow how an
algorithm climbs the log-likelihood step by step. The last part of the page is about
hypothesis tests, which we do not use in this course.
:::

# Uncertainty from the likelihood {#sec-likelihood-uncertainty}

In [Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd#sec-standard_errors) we reported the uncertainty of
an estimate with a standard error and a confidence interval, and for the mean of Poisson
counts we had a formula for the standard error. For most models and parameters there is no
such formula. In this section we calculate standard errors and confidence intervals from
the likelihood itself, which we can do for any model that we fit with `optim()`.

A confidence interval can be calculated from a likelihood in (at least) two ways. The
**Wald interval** uses the asymptotic normality of the MLE and the curvature of the
log-likelihood at its maximum. The **likelihood profile interval** uses the whole shape of
the log-likelihood around the maximum. In this book the likelihood profile interval is the
better method in general, but the Wald interval is the fast approximation that software
usually reports. This section explains both, shows when they differ and checks their
coverage by simulation.

## Standard errors and Wald intervals

In [Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd#sec-confidence_intervals) we defined the Wald
interval^[The interval is named after Abraham Wald, who developed in 1943 the large-sample
test on which it is based.] as $\hat\theta\pm z_{0.975}\,\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\theta)$
and justified it with the approximately Normal sampling distribution of the estimator.
[Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd#sec-large_samples) ended with the asymptotic normality
of estimators, and it also applies to maximum likelihood estimators: as the sample grows,
the sampling distribution of an MLE approaches a Normal distribution centred on the
parameter.^[Fisher used the large-sample standard error of maximum likelihood estimators
in 1922 and developed the concept of information in 1925, with arguments that were not
rigorous. The result was made rigorous by Wald (1943) and by Cramér (1946), whose
treatment states the conditions explicitly.] For one parameter:

$$
\hat\theta \overset{\mathrm{approx}}{\sim}
\operatorname{Normal}\left(\theta,\operatorname{SE}(\hat\theta)^2\right)
\quad\text{for sufficiently large }n,
$$

where $\operatorname{SE}(\hat\theta)$ is the standard error of the estimator, that is, the
standard deviation of its sampling distribution. In plain English, across large
hypothetical samples^[These results require some conditions on the model, known as
regularity conditions. In words: the parameter is not on the boundary of its range (e.g.,
a variance of exactly zero), the support of the distribution does not depend on the
parameter, the log-likelihood is a smooth function of the parameters, and the number of
parameters does not grow with the sample size.] the estimates fall around the parameter in
the shape of a bell.

With several parameters, the estimates jointly follow approximately a **multivariate
Normal distribution**, which extends the bivariate Normal distribution of
[Chapter 2](../Chapter_2/Theory.qmd#sec-two_continuous_variables) to any number of
variables (see the
[supplement entry](../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-multivariate_normal)). Its means
are the parameters of the model, and its **covariance matrix** contains the variance of the
estimator of each parameter on the diagonal and the covariance between the estimators of
each pair of parameters outside the diagonal. The Wald interval of one parameter uses only
its variance, through the standard error, which is the square root of the variance. What
maximum likelihood adds to Chapter 3 is a way to estimate this covariance matrix from the
log-likelihood of the sample, for any model, also when there is no formula for the
variance of the estimator.

### Curvature and standard errors {#sec-curvature}

The Normal approximation of the sampling distribution has a counterpart in the shape of
the log-likelihood: in a large sample the log-likelihood near its maximum is close to a
parabola,

$$
\ell(\theta)-\ell(\hat\theta)\approx
-\frac{(\theta-\hat\theta)^2}{2\,\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\theta)^2},
$$

that is, a polynomial of degree two in the parameter, with its maximum at the estimate and
a width set by the standard error. With several parameters it is a polynomial of degree two
in all of them, with a squared term for each parameter and a product term for each pair.
The two approximations go together, and the Wald interval relies on both: it amounts to
replacing the log-likelihood by this parabola, which is why it is also called a quadratic
interval.

The **curvature** of the log-likelihood at its maximum measures how fast the log-likelihood
falls as we move away from the estimate, and it determines the standard error. A
log-likelihood that falls slowly has a small curvature: many parameter values are almost
equally well supported by the data, which corresponds to a large standard error. A
log-likelihood that falls quickly has a large curvature: the data discriminate well among
parameter values, and the standard error is small. For one parameter the relation follows
from the parabola above, whose curvature is
$1/\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\theta)^2$^[Mathematically the curvature is given by the negative of the second derivative]. That is, the standard error is one over the
square root of the curvature, so a log-likelihood that is four times as sharply curved
gives half the standard error. A larger sample contains more information about the
parameter, which gives a more sharply curved log-likelihood and a smaller standard error.

With several parameters, the curvatures of the log-likelihood along each parameter and for
each pair of parameters give the whole covariance matrix of the estimates. The tilted
contours of the surface in the parameterisation with $k$ and $p$ (@fig-slice_profile) are
an example: they describe estimates that are correlated. The boxes below give the
mathematics of these statements.

The approximation is good when the log-likelihood is close to a parabola on the scale of the
parameter. When it is not, for example when the log-likelihood is asymmetric like the curve
of the ten quadrats (@fig-likelihood_curve), the standard error describes only the
curvature at the maximum and the Wald interval is less accurate.

::: {.callout-note title="Asymptotic normality of maximum likelihood estimators"}
For a large sample of i.i.d. observations from the model, the sampling distribution of
maximum likelihood estimators is approximately (multivariate) Normal and centred on the
parameters. Its covariance matrix is estimated from the curvature of the log-likelihood at
its maximum: the more sharply curved the log-likelihood, the smaller the standard errors.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true" icon=false title="Statistical detail: Fisher information"}
The curvature of the log-likelihood at the estimate is the **observed information**, which
is the negative of its second derivative there. Its inverse estimates the variance of the
estimator:

$$
\hat{\mathcal I}=-\ell''(\hat\theta),
\qquad
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\theta)=\frac{1}{\hat{\mathcal I}},
\qquad
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\theta)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\hat{\mathcal I}}}.
$$

The asymptotic result is usually stated with the **Fisher information**
$\mathcal I(\theta)$, also called the **expected information**: the expectation of
$-\ell''(\theta)$ across hypothetical samples, which measures how much information a sample
of this size contains about $\theta$. Then

$$
\hat\theta \overset{\mathrm{approx}}{\sim}
\operatorname{Normal}\left(\theta,\frac{1}{\mathcal I(\theta)}\right)
\quad\text{for sufficiently large }n.
$$

The observed information is calculated from the log-likelihood of the sample that we have,
and the two agree in large samples.^[Efron and Hinkley (1978) compared them and argued for
the observed information.] In plain English, the more information the sample contains, the
narrower the bell of the sampling distribution.

For the Poisson model the calculation can be done by hand. The second derivative of its
log-likelihood is $\ell''(\lambda)=-\sum x_i/\lambda^2$ (see the box of
@sec-maximum-likelihood). At $\hat\lambda=\overline x$ the sum of the counts is
$n\hat\lambda$, so for the ten quadrats

$$
\hat{\mathcal I}=\frac{n\hat\lambda}{\hat\lambda^2}=\frac{n}{\hat\lambda}=\frac{10}{2.2}\approx 4.55,
\qquad
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\lambda)=\frac{\hat\lambda}{n}=0.22,
\qquad
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\lambda)=\sqrt{0.22}\approx 0.47.
$$

The result, $\sqrt{\hat\lambda/n}$, is the plug-in standard error that we obtained in
[Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd#sec-standard_errors) from the variance of a mean. For
all 50 quadrats it gives the 0.21 seedlings per quadrat of that chapter.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true" icon=false title="Statistical detail: the Hessian matrix"}
With several parameters the observed information is a matrix. The matrix of second
derivatives of a function is called its **Hessian**, and the Hessian of the NLL at the
estimates is the observed information matrix. For two parameters $\theta_1$ and
$\theta_2$,

$$
\mathbf H=
\begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial^2(-\ell)}{\partial\theta_1^2} &
\dfrac{\partial^2(-\ell)}{\partial\theta_1\,\partial\theta_2}\\[2ex]
\dfrac{\partial^2(-\ell)}{\partial\theta_2\,\partial\theta_1} &
\dfrac{\partial^2(-\ell)}{\partial\theta_2^2}
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\hat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}=\mathbf H^{-1},
$$

where the derivatives are evaluated at the estimates (see the
[calculus supplement](../Supplements/calculus.qmd) for partial derivatives) and
$\hat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}$ is the estimate of the covariance matrix of the estimates. In
plain English, the inverse of the Hessian has the variances of the estimates on its
diagonal and their covariances outside it. The elements outside the diagonal of the
Hessian measure how the slope of the NLL along one parameter changes with the other
parameter, which is what makes the contours of a likelihood surface tilted.

The Hessian refers to the parameters that the optimiser searched over. For the ten
quadrats, written in terms of $\log(\lambda)$, the NLL is
$\sum_i\left(e^{\log(\lambda)}-x_i\log(\lambda)\right)$ plus a constant, so its second
derivative with respect to $\log(\lambda)$ is $n\lambda$. At the estimate this is
$10\times 2.2=22$, and the standard error of the estimate of $\log(\lambda)$ is
$1/\sqrt{22}\approx 0.213$.

In R, `optim()` returns a numerical Hessian of the function that it minimised when it is
called with `hessian = TRUE`, and `solve()` inverts a matrix. `sdreport()` does both steps
for us, so we use it instead (the practical takes the Hessian from `optim()` once, for
comparison).
:::

### Standard errors with TMB {#sec-wald-automation}

The function `sdreport()` of RTMB calculates the standard errors of any model processed
with `MakeADFun()`. It takes the object after the fit (it reads the estimates from the
object), calculates the curvature of the NLL at the estimates and converts it into the
covariance matrix of the estimates. `summary()` of its result is a table with one row per
parameter, on the scale that was optimised, and two columns:

- `Estimate`, the estimate of the parameter;
- `Std. Error`, its standard error.

For the ten quadrats, the parameter that was optimised is $\log(\lambda)$:

```{r}
# sdreport() calculates the standard errors from the curvature at the estimates.
summary(sdreport(fir_ten_obj))
```

The object returned by `sdreport()` also keeps the covariance matrix of the estimates in its
element `cov.fixed`. A covariance divided by the two standard errors is the correlation
between the estimates, which
[Chapter 2](../Chapter_2/Theory.qmd#sec-two_continuous_variables) introduced as a parameter
of the bivariate Normal distribution, and `cov2cor()` does this conversion for a whole
matrix. For the owl model we calculate the correlation in both parameterisations of
@fig-slice_profile:

```{r}
# Standard errors of log(mu) and log(k), and the correlation between their estimates.
owl_sd = sdreport(owl_obj)
summary(owl_sd)
cov2cor(owl_sd$cov.fixed)

# The correlation in the parameterisation with k and p.
cov2cor(sdreport(owl_prob_obj)$cov.fixed)
```

For the estimates of $\log(\mu)$ and $\log(k)$ the correlation is zero to four decimals,
because the contours of @fig-likelihood_surface are not tilted. For those of $\log(k)$ and
$\operatorname{logit}(p)$ it is 0.71: hypothetical samples that overestimate $k$ would also
tend to overestimate $p$. This is the tilt of the contours in @fig-slice_profile expressed
as a number.

### Standard errors on the original scale {#sec-wald-constrained}

The standard errors of `sdreport()` refer to the scale that was optimised. For the ten
quadrats this is the standard error of the estimate of $\log(\lambda)$, 0.213, and not of
$\hat\lambda$. The estimate can be transformed back with `exp()`, because by invariance the
result is the MLE of $\lambda$. The standard error cannot: `exp(0.213)` is 1.24, which is not
a standard error of $\hat\lambda$. It could not have been one, because the exponential of a
positive number is always larger than one, so it would stay above 1 seedling per quadrat
however many quadrats we sampled, whereas a standard error becomes smaller as the sample
grows.

The reason is that a non-linear function does not pass through an average. For a
non-linear function $g$ and a random variable $X$ that varies, in general

$$
E[g(X)]\neq g(E[X]).
$$

In plain English, the mean of a transformed variable is not the transformation of the mean.
A variance is an average, the expectation of the squared distance from the mean (see
[Chapter 2](../Chapter_2/Theory.qmd#sec-expectations)), and a standard error is its square
root, so neither of them can be carried to a new scale by
applying the transformation to it. An estimate and the endpoints of an interval are values
of the parameter and not averages, which is why they can be transformed back.

The standard error on the new scale is calculated instead with the **delta method**, which
treats the transformation as a straight line near the estimate and multiplies the standard
error by the slope of that line. It is an approximation, because the transformation is not
a straight line, but it is good when the standard error is small and it is widely used.
The box on the delta method below gives its formula, and
[Chapter 6](../Chapter_6/Theory.qmd#sec-delta-method) applies it to a fitted curve, a
quantity that depends on several parameters. In TMB we
ask for it with the function `ADREPORT()`. Placed inside the NLL, `ADREPORT(x)` tells
`sdreport()` to report the quantity `x`, calculated from the parameters, with its
standard error: TMB applies the delta method and adds a row for `x` to the table.

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true" icon=false title="Statistical detail: Jensen's inequality"}
**Jensen's inequality** gives the direction of the difference between $E[g(X)]$ and
$g(E[X])$: $E[g(X)]\ge g(E[X])$ if $g$ is convex (its curve bends upwards, as the
exponential does) and $E[g(X)]\le g(E[X])$ if $g$ is concave (its curve bends downwards, as
the logarithm does). So the curvature of the function decides the sign of the difference,
but the difference exists for any non-linear function. For example, if $X$ takes the values
0 and 2 with equal probabilities, the exponential of its mean is $\exp(1)\approx 2.72$,
whereas the mean of its exponential is $(\exp(0)+\exp(2))/2\approx 4.19$.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true" icon=false title="Statistical detail: the delta method"}
The delta method uses the first derivative of the transformation $g$ at the estimate (see
the [rules of differentiation](../Supplements/calculus.qmd#sec-calc-rules) of the calculus
supplement), which tells us how much the function stretches small differences around the
estimate:

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(g(\hat\theta))\approx
\left|g'(\hat\theta)\right|\,\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\theta).
$$

In plain English, the standard error on the new scale is approximately the standard error
on the old scale multiplied by the slope of the transformation at the estimate. Each
transformation therefore has its own correction:

- For a log-transformed parameter, the transformation back is the exponential, whose
  derivative is the exponential itself. The delta method multiplies the standard error on
  the log scale by the estimate: for the ten quadrats,
  $\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\lambda)\approx\hat\lambda\,\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\log(\hat\lambda))=2.2\times 0.213\approx 0.47$,
  the standard error of the box on Fisher information.^[The two numbers agree exactly
  because both come from the curvature of the same log-likelihood at its maximum. Both are
  still large-sample approximations of the standard deviation of $\hat\lambda$ across
  hypothetical samples.]
- For a probability fitted on the logit scale, the transformation back is the inverse logit,
  $p=1/(1+e^{-\operatorname{logit}(p)})$, whose derivative is $p(1-p)$. The delta method
  multiplies the standard error on the logit scale by $\hat p(1-\hat p)$.

For a quantity that depends on several parameters the slope becomes a vector of partial
derivatives, which is combined with the covariance matrix of the estimates
([Chapter 6](../Chapter_6/Theory.qmd#sec-delta-method)).
:::

For the ten quadrats we add one line to the Poisson NLL, `ADREPORT(lambda)`, which asks
for the standard error of $\lambda$ itself. `sdreport()` reads the estimates from the
processed object, so we process the new NLL and fit it again (the estimate does not change)
before we call it:

```{r}
# The Poisson NLL with one more line.
poisson_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  lambda = exp(log_lambda)
  # Ask for the standard error of lambda itself.
  ADREPORT(lambda)
  -sum(dpois(x = counts, lambda = lambda, log = TRUE))
}

# Process the new NLL for the ten quadrats, fit it again and calculate the standard errors.
fir_ten_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(poisson_nll, list(counts = ten_counts)),
  list(log_lambda = log(1)),
  silent = TRUE
)
fir_ten_fit = optim(
  par = fir_ten_obj$par,
  fn = fir_ten_obj$fn,
  gr = fir_ten_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
fir_ten_summary = summary(sdreport(fir_ten_obj))
fir_ten_summary
```

The last row is the quantity that we asked for with `ADREPORT()`. Its standard error, 0.47
seedlings per quadrat, is the estimate multiplied by the standard error of
$\log(\hat\lambda)$, $2.2\times 0.213$, as the delta method for the exponential says. For
the owl model we add `ADREPORT(k)` in the same way:

```{r}
# The Negative Binomial NLL with one more line.
nb_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  mu = exp(log_mu)
  k = exp(log_k)
  # Ask for the standard error of k itself.
  ADREPORT(k)
  -sum(dnbinom2(x = calls, mu = mu, size = k, log = TRUE))
}

# Process the new NLL, fit it again and calculate the standard errors.
owl_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(nb_nll, list(calls = call_counts)),
  list(log_mu = log(mu_mom), log_k = log(k_mom)),
  silent = TRUE
)
owl_fit = optim(par = owl_obj$par, fn = owl_obj$fn, gr = owl_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
owl_sd = sdreport(owl_obj)
owl_summary = summary(owl_sd)
owl_summary
```

The standard error of $\hat k$ in the last row, 0.054, is again the estimate multiplied by
the standard error of $\log(\hat k)$, $0.327\times 0.165$.

### Wald intervals on the original and log scales {#sec-wald-intervals}

With a standard error on each scale we can calculate a Wald interval for $\lambda$ in two
ways: on the original scale, from the row `lambda`, or on the log scale, from the row
`log_lambda`, with its endpoints transformed back with `exp()`. Unlike a standard error,
the endpoints of an interval can be transformed directly:^[That is because the logarithm
is an increasing function: $\log(\lambda)$ lies between the two endpoints on the log scale
exactly when $\lambda$ lies between their exponentials. So the interval contains the
parameter in the same hypothetical samples on both scales, and its coverage is kept.]

```{r}
# Wald intervals for the Poisson mean of the ten quadrats, in seedlings per quadrat.
critical_value = qnorm(p = 0.975)

# On the original scale, from the row of ADREPORT().
wald_original = fir_ten_summary["lambda", "Estimate"] +
  c(-1, 1) * critical_value * fir_ten_summary["lambda", "Std. Error"]

# On the log scale, with the endpoints transformed back.
wald_log = exp(
  fir_ten_summary["log_lambda", "Estimate"] +
    c(-1, 1) * critical_value * fir_ten_summary["log_lambda", "Std. Error"]
)

rbind(wald_original, wald_log)
```

The interval from the log scale (1.45 to 3.34 seedlings per quadrat) differs from the
interval on the original scale (1.28 to 3.12), although both are 95% Wald intervals for the
same parameter and the same data. This is not due to the back-transformation of the
endpoints but because Wald intervals rely on the sampling distribution being Normal, and how
well this holds depends on the scale of the parameter. The sampling distribution of a
parameter that was transformed to make it unconstrained approaches the Normal distribution
faster (in terms of sample size) than on the original scale, because constraints on
parameter values make sampling distributions skewed when the standard error is relatively
large. In terms of the log-likelihood, the curve is closer to a parabola when the parameter is on the log scale.
So the transformation of parameters is not only useful for the optimisation algorithm, it
also makes Wald intervals more reliable, and we calculate them on the scale that was
optimised. We do the same for the owl model, where we also calculate the interval for $k$
on the original scale, from the row of `ADREPORT()`:

```{r}
# Lower and upper endpoints of a Wald interval for every row of the table.
owl_lower = owl_summary[, "Estimate"] - critical_value * owl_summary[, "Std. Error"]
owl_upper = owl_summary[, "Estimate"] + critical_value * owl_summary[, "Std. Error"]

# Rows log_mu and log_k: intervals on the log scales, with the endpoints transformed back.
owl_wald_mu = exp(c(owl_lower[["log_mu"]], owl_upper[["log_mu"]]))
owl_wald_k = exp(c(owl_lower[["log_k"]], owl_upper[["log_k"]]))

# Row k, from ADREPORT(): interval for k on the original scale.
owl_wald_k_original = c(owl_lower[["k"]], owl_upper[["k"]])
```

We compare these intervals with the likelihood profile intervals in
@sec-profile_intervals.

:::: {#imp-log-scale-interval .callout-important title="an interval from the log scale"}

In @imp-ecological-scale, about ticks on lizards, the fit on the log scale returned `par = 0.92`.
For that parameter, `sdreport()` reports a standard error of 0.141. Calculate a 95%
Wald interval for the mean number of ticks per lizard. Why is it not symmetric around the
estimate?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

The standard error is that of the estimate of the logarithm of the mean, so we calculate
the interval on the log scale and transform its endpoints:

```{r}
# Wald interval on the log scale, back-transformed to ticks per lizard.
exp(0.92 + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(p = 0.975) * 0.141)
```

The interval goes from approximately 1.9 to 3.3 ticks per lizard, around an estimate of
2.5. It is symmetric on the log scale, and `exp()` stretches the part above the estimate
more than the part below it.

:::
::::

## Likelihood profile intervals {#sec-profile_intervals}

The Wald interval uses the curvature of the log-likelihood at one point, its maximum. The
likelihood profile interval uses the whole curve: it contains all the values of the
parameter whose relative profile log-likelihood is above a cutoff, that is, the values
that the data support almost as well as the estimate. The cutoff is chosen so that, in a
large sample, the interval contains the parameter in approximately 95% of hypothetical
samples. It is half the 0.95 quantile of a **chi-squared distribution** with one degree of
freedom, a result known as Wilks' theorem (stated in the box below). In R, the quantiles of
a chi-squared distribution are calculated with `qchisq()`:

```{r}
# Cutoff for the relative profile log-likelihood: half the 95% quantile of a
# chi-squared distribution with one degree of freedom.
cutoff = qchisq(p = 0.95, df = 1) / 2
cutoff
```

::: {.callout-note title="Likelihood profile interval"}
An approximate 95% confidence interval for a parameter contains all the values whose
profile log-likelihood is within 1.92 units of the maximum log-likelihood (half the 0.95
quantile of a chi-squared distribution with one degree of freedom). The other parameters
of the model are re-estimated for each value.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true" icon=false title="Statistical detail: Wilks' theorem"}
The cutoff of the likelihood profile interval comes from
**Wilks' theorem**,^[Wilks (1938). The theorem is about the ratio between two maximised
likelihoods (a difference between two log-likelihoods is the logarithm of a likelihood
ratio), and it holds under the regularity conditions that asymptotic normality requires.
The likelihood profile interval follows from it.] which describes how far below its
maximum the log-likelihood is at the parameter value that generated the data. Let
$\theta_0$ be that value for the parameter of interest. Then

$$
2\left[\ell(\hat\theta)-\ell_{\mathrm{prof}}(\theta_0)\right]
\overset{\mathrm{approx}}{\sim}\chi^2_1
\quad\text{for sufficiently large }n,
$$

where $\ell(\hat\theta)$ is the maximum of the log-likelihood,
$\ell_{\mathrm{prof}}(\theta_0)$ is the profile log-likelihood at $\theta_0$ (with a single
parameter it is the log-likelihood itself) and $\chi^2_1$ is the chi-squared distribution
with one degree of freedom, which is the distribution of the square of a standard Normal
variable. In plain English, across hypothetical samples the parameter value that
generated the data is rarely far down the slope of the profile: twice its distance to the
top behaves like the square of a standard Normal variable.^[The same result is the basis
of the likelihood ratio test, which compares two nested models by calculating a p-value
from the chi-squared distribution. As with p-values in general, we do not use it in this
course.] So in about 95% of hypothetical samples the profile log-likelihood at $\theta_0$
is within $3.84/2=1.92$ units of the maximum. The likelihood profile interval contains
$\theta_0$ in exactly those samples, which gives it a coverage of approximately 95%.
:::

The calculation of a likelihood profile interval follows the same two steps for every
model and parameter. First, the profile: the parameter of interest is moved away from its
estimate in small steps, the other parameters are re-estimated at each step by an
optimisation of their own (an **inner fit**), and the NLL is recorded. With a single
parameter there is nothing to re-estimate, and the profile is the log-likelihood itself.
Second, the endpoints: the two values of the parameter, one below and one above the
