estimate, at which the relative profile log-likelihood crosses the cutoff. We do not
program these steps ourselves, because two functions do them:

- `TMB::tmbprofile()` calculates the profile of one parameter of a model that was
  processed with `MakeADFun()`. Its main arguments are the object and `name`, the name of
  the parameter to profile as it is written in the list of parameters; `trace = FALSE`
  stops the printing of progress. It returns a data frame with the values of the parameter
  and the NLL at each of them. The function belongs to the package TMB, on which RTMB is
  built and which is installed with it, so we write `TMB::tmbprofile()`.
- `confint()` takes the result of `tmbprofile()` and finds the two crossings of the
  cutoff, that is, the endpoints of the 95% likelihood profile interval.

The profile is calculated on the scale that was optimised, so we transform the endpoints
back.

### One parameter

The Poisson model has one parameter, so the endpoints of the interval are the two values
of $\lambda$ at which the relative log-likelihood of the ten quadrats equals $-1.92$. We
profile `log_lambda` in the object of the ten quadrats and collect the interval with the
two Wald intervals:

```{r}
# Profile of log(lambda) for the ten quadrats and its 95% interval, transformed back.
fir_ten_profile = TMB::tmbprofile(fir_ten_obj, name = "log_lambda", trace = FALSE)
likelihood_interval = exp(confint(fir_ten_profile))

# The three intervals for lambda (seedlings per quadrat) from the ten quadrats.
intervals_ten = rbind(wald_original, wald_log, likelihood_interval)
dimnames(intervals_ten) = list(
  c("Wald, original scale", "Wald, log scale", "Likelihood"),
  c("lower", "upper")
)
intervals_ten
```

The likelihood interval is not symmetric: it extends 0.80 below the estimate and 1.05
above it, following the asymmetry of the curve (@fig-profile_interval). It also does not
depend on the scale, because a value of $\lambda$ and its logarithm have the same
likelihood: `tmbprofile()` searched over $\log(\lambda)$, and the transformed endpoints are
exactly the values of $\lambda$ at which the curve of @fig-profile_interval crosses the
cutoff. The Wald interval on the original
scale is the interval of the parabola: because $z_{0.975}^2/2=1.92$, the parabola crosses
the cutoff exactly at its endpoints. Where the curve is not a parabola, as on the left of
the estimate, the two intervals disagree. The Wald interval from the log scale is closer to
the likelihood interval, as expected from the previous section.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-profile_interval
#| fig-cap: "Relative log-likelihood of the counts of fir seedlings in the first ten quadrats (solid line) and its quadratic approximation on the original scale (dashed line). The horizontal line is the cutoff of the 95% interval, at -1.92. The likelihood interval contains the values where the curve is above the cutoff (dotted lines), and the Wald interval on the original scale those where the parabola is above it."
# Quadratic approximation with the same curvature at the maximum, from the standard error
# of lambda in the row of ADREPORT().
se_lambda_ten = fir_ten_summary["lambda", "Std. Error"]
quadratic_values = -(lambda_grid - lambda_hat_ten)^2 / (2 * se_lambda_ten^2)
profile_figure_data = rbind(
  data.frame(lambda = lambda_grid, relative = relative_loglik, curve = "Log-likelihood"),
  data.frame(lambda = lambda_grid, relative = quadratic_values, curve = "Quadratic approximation")
)
ggplot(profile_figure_data, aes(x = lambda, y = relative, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -cutoff, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = as.vector(likelihood_interval),
    colour = "grey40",
    linetype = "dotted"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-6, 0)) +
  labs(
    x = expression(paste("Mean seedlings per quadrat, ", lambda)),
    y = "Relative log-likelihood",
    linetype = NULL
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

```{r}
#| include: false
# The three intervals for all 50 quadrats, with the NLL that reports lambda.
fir_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(poisson_nll, list(counts = seedling_counts)),
  list(log_lambda = log(1)),
  silent = TRUE
)
fir_fit = optim(par = fir_obj$par, fn = fir_obj$fn, gr = fir_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
fir_summary = summary(sdreport(fir_obj))
wald_original_all = fir_summary["lambda", "Estimate"] +
  c(-1, 1) * critical_value * fir_summary["lambda", "Std. Error"]
wald_log_all = exp(
  fir_summary["log_lambda", "Estimate"] +
    c(-1, 1) * critical_value * fir_summary["log_lambda", "Std. Error"]
)
fir_profile = TMB::tmbprofile(fir_obj, name = "log_lambda", trace = FALSE)
rbind(wald_original_all, wald_log_all, exp(confint(fir_profile)))
```

With all 50 quadrats the three intervals nearly coincide: 1.73 to 2.55 seedlings per
quadrat for the Wald interval on the original scale (the interval of
[Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd#sec-confidence_intervals)), 1.77 to 2.59 from the log
scale and 1.76 to 2.57 for the likelihood interval. The log-likelihood of a larger sample
is closer to a parabola around its maximum, so the quadratic approximation behind the Wald
interval is better, and it hardly matters which interval we report.

### Two parameters

The owl model has two parameters, so the interval of each of them is calculated from its
profile (@sec-likelihood-surface). At each value of $\log(k)$ that it visits,
`tmbprofile()` makes an inner fit that re-estimates $\log(\mu)$, and the other way round
when we profile $\log(\mu)$. We do this for both parameters and collect the results with
the Wald intervals:

```{r}
# Profiles of log(mu) and log(k), and their 95% intervals transformed back.
owl_profile_mu = TMB::tmbprofile(owl_obj, name = "log_mu", trace = FALSE)
owl_profile_k = TMB::tmbprofile(owl_obj, name = "log_k", trace = FALSE)
owl_interval_mu = exp(confint(owl_profile_mu))
owl_interval_k = exp(confint(owl_profile_k))

# Profile intervals next to the Wald intervals.
owl_intervals = rbind(
  owl_interval_mu, owl_wald_mu, owl_interval_k, owl_wald_k, owl_wald_k_original
)
dimnames(owl_intervals) = list(
  c("mu, profile", "mu, Wald from the log scale",
    "k, profile", "k, Wald from the log scale", "k, Wald on the original scale"),
  c("lower", "upper")
)
owl_intervals
```

For both parameters the Wald interval from the log scale is close to the likelihood profile
interval (0.237 to 0.453 against 0.235 to 0.451 for $k$). The Wald interval for $k$ on the
original scale (0.221 to 0.434) is not: it is symmetric around the estimate, whereas the
likelihood profile interval extends further above the estimate than below it, so both of
its endpoints are too low. This is why we calculate Wald intervals on the scale that was
optimised and transform their endpoints, and why the likelihood profile interval is the
reference with which we compare them.

## Joint confidence regions

A **joint confidence region** is the counterpart of a confidence interval for two
parameters at once. It is defined in the same way as the likelihood profile interval, with
a cutoff of 3.00 units of log-likelihood instead of 1.92 (half the 0.95 quantile of a
chi-squared distribution with two degrees of freedom, `qchisq(p = 0.95, df = 2) / 2`). The
combinations of $\mu$ and $k$ whose relative log-likelihood is above $-3.00$ form an
approximate 95% joint confidence region, which is the area inside one contour of the
likelihood surface (@fig-joint_region). The region extends beyond the likelihood profile
interval of each parameter, because it answers a question about both parameters at once:
in about 95% of hypothetical samples it contains the pair of values that generated the
data, which is more demanding than containing one of them. We use an interval when a
question is about one parameter and a region when it is about a combination of parameters.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-joint_region
#| fig-cap: "Approximate joint 95% confidence region for the mean and the shape of the Negative Binomial model fitted to the owl data (contour in vermillion). The segments along the axes are the 95% likelihood profile intervals of each parameter."
# Cutoff for a joint region of two parameters: half the 95% quantile of a chi-squared
# distribution with two degrees of freedom (qchisq(p = 0.95, df = 2) is 5.99).
joint_cutoff = qchisq(p = 0.95, df = 2) / 2

# Contours of the surface, the contour of the joint region, the estimate and the
# profile intervals of the two parameters drawn along the axes.
ggplot() +
  geom_contour(
    data = surface_data,
    aes(x = mu, y = k, z = relative),
    breaks = c(-12, -9, -6, -4, -2, -1),
    colour = "grey40"
  ) +
  geom_contour(
    data = surface_data,
    aes(x = mu, y = k, z = relative),
    breaks = -joint_cutoff,
    colour = "#D55E00",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = data.frame(mu = mu_mle, k = k_mle),
    aes(x = mu, y = k),
    colour = "#D55E00",
    size = 3
  ) +
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = owl_interval_mu[1, "lower"], xend = owl_interval_mu[1, "upper"],
    y = min(k_grid), yend = min(k_grid),
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = min(mu_grid), xend = min(mu_grid),
    y = owl_interval_k[1, "lower"], yend = owl_interval_k[1, "upper"],
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  labs(
    x = expression(paste("Mean number of calls per visit, ", mu)),
    y = expression(paste("Shape, ", italic(k)))
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true" icon=false title="Statistical detail: the cutoff for a joint region"}
Wilks' theorem also applies to several parameters at once. If we fix two parameters at the
same time, twice the drop in log-likelihood from the maximum follows approximately a
chi-squared distribution with two degrees of freedom (the distribution of the sum of the
squares of two independent standard Normal variables). The cutoff for the joint region is
half its 0.95 quantile (5.99), `qchisq(p = 0.95, df = 2) / 2`.

A likelihood profile interval is a statement about one parameter, whatever the value of
the other: it is the range that the contour at $-1.92$ covers along one axis. Capturing
two parameters simultaneously is more demanding than capturing one, so the cutoff of the
joint region is further from the maximum. Note that the joint region is not the rectangle
formed by the two separate intervals: the shape of the likelihood contours matters.
:::

## Coverage checked by simulation

As in [Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd#sec-confidence_intervals), we check the coverage
of the intervals with a simulation in which we know the parameters. To simulate from a
model that is written as an NLL, we mark the data inside it with `OBS()`. The object
returned by `MakeADFun()` then has a function `simulate()`, which draws one hypothetical
sample of the size of the data for the parameter values that we give it, on the scale
that was optimised:

```{r}
# The complete NLL of the Negative Binomial model.
nb_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  # Mark the data as observations, so that they can be simulated.
  calls = OBS(calls)
  mu = exp(log_mu)
  k = exp(log_k)
  ADREPORT(k)
  -sum(dnbinom2(x = calls, mu = mu, size = k, log = TRUE))
}
```

We process and fit it as before (the estimates do not change) and give `simulate()` the
estimates on the log scale, which are in the element `par` of the fit. It returns a list
in which the simulated data have the name that they have in the NLL (`calls`). For
example, these are the first 20 counts of one hypothetical sample of 122 visits:

```{r}
# Process and fit as before.
owl_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(nb_nll, list(calls = call_counts)),
  list(log_mu = log(mu_mom), log_k = log(k_mom)),
  silent = TRUE
)
owl_fit = optim(par = owl_obj$par, fn = owl_obj$fn, gr = owl_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")

# One hypothetical sample of 122 visits at the estimates: its first 20 counts.
set.seed(seed = 700)
owl_obj$simulate(owl_fit$par)$calls[1:20]
```

For each hypothetical sample we calculate both types of interval and record whether each
of them contains the parameter used to simulate (the code is not shown). We consider two
cases with small samples, where the coverage of the intervals is not guaranteed
(@fig-coverage). The first uses a Poisson model with a mean of 0.5 seedlings per quadrat and
5,000 hypothetical samples of ten quadrats, and compares the Wald interval on the original
scale with the likelihood interval. The coverage of the Wald interval is 0.878, far from the
intended 0.95, and that of the likelihood interval is 0.924.^[A sample in which all the
quadrats are empty gives an estimate of zero. The Wald interval on the original scale then
collapses to $[0,0]$. The simulation counts such a sample as a miss for both intervals; it
happens in less than 1% of these samples.] The second uses the Negative Binomial model with
the owl estimates as parameters and 2,000 hypothetical samples of 20 visits, and compares,
for the shape $k$, the Wald interval calculated on the log scale with the likelihood
profile interval. The coverages are 0.945 and 0.942, so here the two intervals perform
equally well.

```{r}
#| include: false
#| warning: false
# Poisson model: coverage of the Wald interval on the original scale and of the
# likelihood interval, for a mean of 0.5 seedlings per quadrat and 10 quadrats.
poisson_sim_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  counts = OBS(counts)
  -sum(dpois(x = counts, lambda = exp(log_lambda), log = TRUE))
}
set.seed(seed = 701)
lambda_sim = 0.5
n_quadrats_sim = 10
# Placeholder data of the right length: the values are not used.
poisson_sim_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(poisson_sim_nll, list(counts = rep(0, times = n_quadrats_sim))),
  list(log_lambda = 0),
  silent = TRUE
)
# The estimate is the mean of the counts, so only the total of each sample is kept.
totals = rep(NA, times = 5000)
for (i in seq_along(totals)) {
  totals[i] = sum(poisson_sim_obj$simulate(log(lambda_sim))$counts)
}
estimates = totals / n_quadrats_sim

# Wald interval on the original scale.
se = sqrt(estimates / n_quadrats_sim)
wald_covered = estimates - critical_value * se <= lambda_sim &
  lambda_sim <= estimates + critical_value * se

# The likelihood interval contains lambda when its relative log-likelihood is within
# the cutoff. A sample of zeros has no finite estimate of the interval: a miss.
relative = -n_quadrats_sim * (lambda_sim - estimates) + totals * log(lambda_sim / estimates)
likelihood_covered = totals > 0 & relative >= -cutoff
coverage_poisson_small = c(wald = mean(wald_covered), likelihood = mean(likelihood_covered))
coverage_poisson_small
mean(totals == 0)

# Negative Binomial model (owl estimates), 20 visits: coverage of the Wald interval for k
# on the log scale and of the profile interval. The profile interval contains the
# generating k when the relative profile log-likelihood at that k is within the cutoff,
# which takes one extra fit with log(k) fixed in place of a whole profile.
set.seed(seed = 702)
n_visits_sim = 20
nb_sim_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(nb_nll, list(calls = rep(0, times = n_visits_sim))),
  list(log_mu = 0, log_k = 0),
  silent = TRUE
)
wald_covered = rep(NA, times = 2000)
profile_covered = rep(NA, times = 2000)
for (i in seq_along(wald_covered)) {
  sim_calls = nb_sim_obj$simulate(owl_fit$par)$calls
  # Starting values: the method-of-moments estimates when they exist.
  sim_mu = mean(sim_calls)
  sim_var = mean((sim_calls - sim_mu)^2)
  k_start = ifelse(sim_var > sim_mu, sim_mu^2 / (sim_var - sim_mu), 1)
  sim_obj = MakeADFun(
    cmb(nb_nll, list(calls = sim_calls)),
    list(log_mu = log(sim_mu), log_k = log(k_start)),
    silent = TRUE
  )
  sim_fit = optim(par = sim_obj$par, fn = sim_obj$fn, gr = sim_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
  se_log_k = tryCatch(
    summary(sdreport(sim_obj))["log_k", "Std. Error"],
    error = function(err) NA
  )
  if (sim_fit$convergence == 0 && !is.na(se_log_k)) {
    wald_covered[i] = abs(log(k_mle) - sim_fit$par[["log_k"]]) <= critical_value * se_log_k
    fixed_obj = MakeADFun(
      cmb(nb_nll, list(calls = sim_calls)),
      list(log_mu = log(sim_mu), log_k = log(k_mle)),
      map = list(log_k = factor(NA)),
      silent = TRUE
    )
    fixed_fit = optim(par = fixed_obj$par, fn = fixed_obj$fn, gr = fixed_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
    profile_covered[i] = sim_fit$value - fixed_fit$value >= -cutoff
  }
}
coverage_nb_small = c(
  wald = mean(wald_covered, na.rm = TRUE),
  profile = mean(profile_covered, na.rm = TRUE),
  failed = sum(is.na(wald_covered))
)
coverage_nb_small

# Collect the results for the figure.
coverage_results = data.frame(
  case = rep(
    c(
      "Poisson, λ = 0.5,\n10 quadrats",
      "Negative Binomial, k,\n20 visits"
    ),
    each = 2
  ),
  interval = rep(c("Wald", "Likelihood"), times = 2),
  coverage = c(
    coverage_poisson_small[["wald"]], coverage_poisson_small[["likelihood"]],
    coverage_nb_small[["wald"]], coverage_nb_small[["profile"]]
  )
)
coverage_results$case = factor(coverage_results$case, levels = unique(coverage_results$case))
coverage_results
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-coverage
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Simulated coverage of nominal 95% Wald and likelihood intervals. Poisson case: 5,000 hypothetical samples, interval for the mean on the original scale. Negative Binomial case: 2,000 hypothetical samples, interval for the shape k, with the Wald interval calculated on the log scale. The dashed line is the nominal level."
# Coverage by case and type of interval; the dashed line is the intended 0.95.
ggplot(coverage_results, aes(x = case, y = coverage, shape = interval, linetype = interval)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.95, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.4),
    colour = "#D55E00",
    size = 3
  ) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "solid")) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.8, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Simulated coverage", shape = NULL) +
  guides(linetype = "none") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

So the Wald interval fails on the original scale when the counts are few, where the
log-likelihood is far from a parabola, and the likelihood interval is clearly better
there. A Wald interval calculated on a suitable scale, such as the logarithm of a positive
parameter, can be just as good as the likelihood profile interval, and it needs one fit
instead of many. In the practical you will run a simulation of this kind for another
model.

::: {.callout-note title="Wald and likelihood profile intervals"}
In this course we prefer likelihood profile intervals, because in small samples their
coverage tends to be closer to the intended 95% than that of Wald intervals: they follow
the shape of the log-likelihood instead of approximating it by a parabola at its maximum.
The price is computation. A Wald interval needs only the fit and its Hessian, whereas a
likelihood profile interval needs one optimisation of the other parameters for every
value of the parameter on the profile, which takes longer and gives more fits that can
fail. When this cost matters, a Wald interval calculated on a scale where the
log-likelihood is close to a parabola (the logarithm of a positive parameter) is a
reasonable approximation.
:::

# Properties of maximum likelihood estimators {#sec-mle_properties}

An MLE is an estimator, so everything that we learnt in
[Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd#sec-sampling_distribution) applies to it: it has a
sampling distribution across hypothetical samples, a bias, a variance and a standard
error, and in a finite sample we do not know that sampling distribution in general. For
large samples, however, the MLEs of a very wide class of models have three properties:
they are consistent and asymptotically normal, like the method-of-moments estimators of
[Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd#sec-large_samples), and in addition they are
asymptotically efficient. These results are the reason why this book uses maximum
likelihood, and the standard errors and intervals of @sec-likelihood-uncertainty rely on
them. In this section we see them at work in one simulation, and we then look at small
samples and at models that do not describe the data generating process.

As in the Chapter 3 practical, we simulate hypothetical samples from the model with the
plug-in estimates as parameters ($\mu=4.75$ and $k=0.327$), 2,000 for each of three sample
sizes: 20, 122 (the size of the owl sample) and 500 visits. `simulate()` draws samples of
the size of the data of its object, so for each sample size we process the NLL with
placeholder data of that length, whose values are not used. Each simulated sample is then
fitted by maximum likelihood, starting from the same values as the placeholder object,
$\log(\mu)=0$ and $\log(k)=0$ (any starting values from which the optimiser reaches the
maximum will do). We keep the estimate of $k$ and the sample itself, which we use again in
@sec-efficiency:

```{r}
#| warning: false
# Hypothetical samples from a Negative Binomial model whose parameters are the
# maximum likelihood estimates for the owls, for three numbers of visits.
set.seed(seed = 601)
n_samples = 2000
visit_sizes = c(20, 122, 500)
sim_k_ml = matrix(NA, nrow = n_samples, ncol = length(visit_sizes))
sim_samples = list()
for (s in seq_along(visit_sizes)) {
  # Placeholder data of the right length: the values are not used.
  placeholder_obj = MakeADFun(
    cmb(nb_nll, list(calls = rep(0, times = visit_sizes[s]))),
    list(log_mu = 0, log_k = 0),
    silent = TRUE
  )
  # One row per hypothetical sample.
  sim_samples[[s]] = matrix(NA, nrow = n_samples, ncol = visit_sizes[s])
  for (i in seq_len(n_samples)) {
    # One hypothetical sample at the estimates for the owls.
    sim_calls = placeholder_obj$simulate(owl_fit$par)$calls
    sim_samples[[s]][i, ] = sim_calls

    # Maximum likelihood, starting from log(mu) = 0 and log(k) = 0.
    sim_obj = MakeADFun(
      cmb(nb_nll, list(calls = sim_calls)),
      list(log_mu = 0, log_k = 0),
      silent = TRUE
    )
    sim_fit = optim(par = sim_obj$par, fn = sim_obj$fn, gr = sim_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
    sim_k_ml[i, s] = exp(sim_fit$par[["log_k"]])
  }
}
```

## Consistency and asymptotic normality

Maximum likelihood estimators are consistent when the observations are i.i.d. from the
model: the chance that the estimate misses the parameter by more than any given margin
becomes small as the sample grows. In the simulation we can calculate the fraction of the
estimates that miss $k$ by 0.1 or more (`colMeans()` takes the mean of each column, one per
sample size, and the mean of `TRUE` and `FALSE` values is the fraction of `TRUE` values):

```{r}
# Fraction of the estimates that differ by 0.1 or more from the shape used to simulate,
# for 20, 122 and 500 visits.
colMeans(abs(sim_k_ml - k_mle) >= 0.1)
```

The fraction is 45% with 20 visits, 7% with 122 visits and zero with 500 visits.

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true" icon=false title="Statistical detail: why maximum likelihood estimators are consistent"}
Why should the maximum of the likelihood be close to the parameter in a large sample (in the
sense of the box on consistency in
[Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd#sec-large_samples))?^[The consistency of maximum
likelihood estimators was proved rigorously, under regularity conditions, by Abraham Wald
(1949).] If we divide the log-likelihood by $n$, which does not move its maximum, we obtain

$$
\frac{1}{n}\ell(\theta)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\left(P(X_i=x_i\mid\theta)\right),
$$

the mean of $\log(P(X=x\mid\theta))$ over the sample. This is an expectation under the
empirical distribution of the sample ([Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd#sec-samples)). As
the sample grows, the empirical distribution converges to the distribution that generated
the data (the Glivenko–Cantelli theorem), so the function that we maximise converges to the
expectation of $\log(P(X=x\mid\theta))$ under that distribution. It can be shown that this
expectation is highest when $\theta$ is the parameter that generated the data (the box on
the Kullback–Leibler divergence in @sec-misspecified says why).
:::

How large the sample needs to be for the Normal approximation of @sec-likelihood-uncertainty
depends on the model and on the parameter (@fig-sampling_distribution_k). With 20 visits
the estimates of $k$ are strongly skewed: half of them are below 0.36, but a long tail to
the right reaches values above 1, and their mean is 0.40, against the 0.327 used to
simulate. With 500 visits their mean is 0.329, their distribution is nearly symmetric and
the Normal curve is close to it.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-sampling_distribution_k
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Maximum likelihood estimates of the shape k from 2,000 hypothetical samples of 20 and of 500 visits, simulated from a Negative Binomial model with the estimates for the owls as parameters. The vertical line is the shape used in the simulation and the curves are Normal distributions with the mean and standard deviation of the estimates."
# Histogram of the estimates for one number of visits, with its Normal approximation.
plot_sampling_k = function(column, bin_width) {
  estimates = sim_k_ml[, column]
  estimate_grid = seq(from = min(estimates), to = max(estimates), length.out = 200)
  approximation = data.frame(
    estimate = estimate_grid,
    density = dnorm(x = estimate_grid, mean = mean(estimates), sd = sd(estimates))
  )
  ggplot(data.frame(estimate = estimates), aes(x = estimate)) +
    geom_histogram(
      aes(y = after_stat(density)),
      binwidth = bin_width,
      fill = "grey90",
      colour = "grey40"
    ) +
    geom_line(
      data = approximation,
      aes(x = estimate, y = density),
      colour = "#D55E00",
      linewidth = 0.8
    ) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = k_mle, linetype = "dashed") +
    labs(
      title = paste(visit_sizes[column], "visits"),
      x = expression(paste("Estimated shape, ", italic(k))),
      y = "Density"
    ) +
    theme_classic()
}

plot_sampling_k(column = 1, bin_width = 0.04) |
  plot_sampling_k(column = 3, bin_width = 0.01)
```

The simulation also checks the standard error of the owl fit. The hypothetical samples of
122 visits have the size of the owl data and were simulated with its estimates, so the
standard deviation of their estimates of $\log(k)$ is what the standard error of
$\log(\hat k)$ from `sdreport()` (0.165) approximates:

```{r}
# Standard deviation of the estimates of log(k) across the hypothetical samples
# of 122 visits (second column of sim_k_ml).
sd(log(sim_k_ml[, 2]))
```

The two agree closely (0.162 against 0.165), so with a sample of this size the standard
error from one fit describes the variation across hypothetical samples well.

## Efficiency {#sec-efficiency}

An estimator is more **efficient** than another estimator of the same parameter when its
estimates vary less across hypothetical samples. This is the property that separates
maximum likelihood from the method of moments. Both estimators of $k$ are consistent, but
they use different information from the sample: the method of moments reproduces the mean
and the variance of the sample, whereas maximum likelihood makes every observed count as
probable as possible. To compare them, we calculate the method-of-moments estimate of $k$
from each of the hypothetical samples that we kept:

```{r}
# Method-of-moments estimates of k from the same hypothetical samples. k exists only
# when the variance is larger than the mean; otherwise the estimate stays NA.
sim_k_mom = matrix(NA, nrow = n_samples, ncol = length(visit_sizes))
for (s in seq_along(visit_sizes)) {
  for (i in seq_len(n_samples)) {
    sim_mu = mean(sim_samples[[s]][i, ])
    sim_var = mean((sim_samples[[s]][i, ] - sim_mu)^2)
    if (sim_var > sim_mu) {
      sim_k_mom[i, s] = sim_mu^2 / (sim_var - sim_mu)
    }
  }
}
```

We then compare the standard deviations and the mean squared errors (MSE,
[Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd#sec-sampling_distribution)) of the two sets of
estimates; in the column names `ml` stands for maximum likelihood and `mom` for the method
of moments:

```{r}
# Standard deviation and mean squared error of both estimators of k for each number of
# visits. na.rm = TRUE skips any sample without a method-of-moments estimate.
efficiency_table = data.frame(
  visits = visit_sizes,
  sd_ml = apply(sim_k_ml, 2, sd),
  sd_mom = apply(sim_k_mom, 2, sd, na.rm = TRUE),
  mse_ml = colMeans((sim_k_ml - k_mle)^2),
  mse_mom = colMeans((sim_k_mom - k_mle)^2, na.rm = TRUE)
)
signif(efficiency_table, digits = 3)
```

With 122 visits the standard deviation of the estimates is 0.055 for maximum likelihood
against 0.086 for the method of moments, and the gap remains with 500 visits (0.024 against
0.042). Standard errors decrease with the square root of the sample size, so the method of
moments would need about $(0.086/0.055)^2\approx 2.5$ times as many visits to estimate $k$
with the precision that maximum likelihood achieves with 122.

What the simulation shows for this model is a general property. An MLE is
**asymptotically efficient**: in large samples no other regular estimator of the same
parameter is more precise, because the variance that an MLE approaches, the one given by
the curvature of the log-likelihood (the inverse of the Fisher information, see the box in
@sec-curvature), is the smallest that such an estimator can have. For your own analysis,
this is the reason to fit a model by maximum likelihood whenever you can write its
likelihood.

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true" icon=false title="Statistical detail: the Cramér–Rao bound"}
How small can the variance of an estimator be?
The **Cramér–Rao bound** states that no unbiased estimator has a variance smaller than the
inverse of the Fisher information:^[The bound was derived independently in the 1940s by
Fréchet, Darmois, Rao and Cramér, and it carries the names of the last two. Fisher had
already obtained a version for large samples in 1925.]

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\tilde\theta)\ge\frac{1}{\mathcal I(\theta)}
\quad\text{for any unbiased estimator }\tilde\theta.
$$

In plain English, the information in a sample sets a limit to the precision with which a
parameter can be estimated from it, whatever the method. The variance of an MLE approaches
this limit as the sample grows, which is what asymptotic efficiency means.
:::

## Bias in finite samples

As for the estimators of Chapter 3, the large-sample results say little about small
samples, where MLEs are in general biased. The relative bias of $\hat k$ in the simulation
is:

```{r}
# Relative bias of the maximum likelihood estimator of k for each number of visits.
data.frame(visits = visit_sizes, relative_bias = colMeans(sim_k_ml) / k_mle - 1)
```

With 20 visits, $\hat k$ is on average 21% larger than the $k$ used to simulate, with 122
visits 2.6% and with 500 visits 0.6%. The bias decreases faster than the standard error as
the sample grows, so in a large sample it is negligible compared with the variation of the
estimates across hypothetical samples.^[Corrections of the bias exist for particular models.
Dividing by $n-1$ in the estimator of a variance is one of them
([Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd#sec-two_parameters)). Restricted maximum likelihood
(REML) is the general approach to reduce the bias of the estimates of variance parameters,
and it is used with the models for grouped observations of
[Chapter 7](../Chapter_7/Theory.qmd#sec-reml).] For a small sample, the properties of this section
are approximations, and simulation is the way to check them.

## Misspecified models {#sec-misspecified}

This section can be skipped at a first reading: the rest of the chapter does not depend on
it. All the properties above assume that the observations are a random sample from the
model. [Chapter 1](../Chapter_1/Theory.qmd) described the model as an approximation of the
data generating process, so this assumption is never exactly right. A model is
**misspecified** when it does not contain the distribution of the data generating process,
whatever the values of its parameters. What does the MLE estimate in that case?

The answer is that, as the sample grows, the MLE converges to the parameter values for
which the model distribution is closest to the distribution of the data generating
process. That is, the fitted model is the best approximation that the model can offer, and
the estimates are the parameters of that approximation (the box below says how closeness
is measured). The standard errors and confidence intervals of @sec-likelihood-uncertainty
are calculated as if the model had generated the data, so with a misspecified model they
are approximations too.

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true" icon=false title="Statistical detail: the Kullback–Leibler divergence"}
The closeness between the model and the data generating process is measured by the
**Kullback–Leibler divergence**,^[Kullback and Leibler (1951) introduced this measure of
"information for discrimination" between two distributions, which is now called the
Kullback–Leibler divergence. Maximum likelihood estimation under a misspecified model is
studied by White (1982), "Maximum likelihood estimation of misspecified models",
*Econometrica*; Huber (1967) is an earlier treatment.] which for a discrete variable is

$$
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\theta)
= E_g\left[\log\left(\frac{g(X)}{P(X\mid\theta)}\right)\right]
= \sum_x g(x)\log\left(\frac{g(x)}{P(X=x\mid\theta)}\right),
$$

where $g(x)$ is the probability with which the data generating process produces the value
$x$, $P(X=x\mid\theta)$ is the probability that the model assigns to it, and $E_g$ is an
expectation ([Chapter 2](../Chapter_2/Theory.qmd#sec-expectations)) calculated with the
probabilities $g$. In plain English, the divergence is the average, over the values that
the data generating process produces, of the logarithm of the ratio between the
probability of a value and the probability that the model gives to it. It is zero when the
model assigns the right probability to every value, and positive otherwise.

This completes the intuition given in the box on consistency. The expectation of
$\log(P(X\mid\theta))$, which the log-likelihood divided by $n$ approaches in a large
sample, is the only part of the divergence that depends on $\theta$, and it enters with a
minus sign. Maximising the likelihood therefore amounts to minimising the divergence
between the model and the data generating process. When the model contains the
distribution that generated the data, the minimum is zero and it is reached at the
parameter that generated them, which is consistency. When it does not, the MLE settles on
the best approximation that the model can offer.
:::

# Model comparison with AIC {#sec-aic}

More than one model can be plausible for the same data.
[Chapter 2](../Chapter_2/Theory.qmd#sec-discrete_distributions) gave heuristics to choose
a distribution and announced formal tools, and the likelihood provides the first of them.
We have compared parameter values of one model through their log-likelihoods, so it is
natural to compare two models through their maximum log-likelihoods. That comparison is
not fair when the models have different numbers of parameters. A model with more
parameters has more freedom to adapt to the particular sample that we collected, including
its accidental features. When one model contains the other as a special case (the Negative
Binomial distribution approaches the Poisson distribution as $k$ grows), its maximum
log-likelihood can never be lower.

The **Akaike information criterion** (AIC) corrects the maximum log-likelihood for the
number of parameters:

$$
\mathrm{AIC}=2K-2\,\ell(\hat\theta),
$$

where $\ell(\hat\theta)$ is the maximum log-likelihood of the model and $K$ is the number
of parameters that were estimated (we write $K$ because $k$ is the shape of the Negative
Binomial distribution). The log-likelihood enters with a minus sign, so among models
fitted to the same data the one with the lowest AIC is preferred. Like the value of a
log-likelihood, the AIC of one model means nothing by itself: only differences between
models fitted to the same observations, in the same units, are meaningful.

A model is an approximation of the data generating process
([Chapter 1](../Chapter_1/Theory.qmd)), and the criterion measures how good that
approximation is. Apart from a constant that is the same for all the models, AIC estimates
how far the fitted model is from the data generating process when the fitted model is used
to predict new data from the same process. The distance is the Kullback–Leibler divergence
of @sec-misspecified.^[Akaike (1973, 1974) derived the criterion as an estimate of a loss
based on the Kullback–Leibler divergence. Reading the term $2K$ as a correction for using
the same data twice is the usual interpretation of the criterion.] The maximum
log-likelihood alone is too optimistic for that purpose, because the same data were used to
fit the model and to evaluate it, and the term $2K$ corrects for this. In plain English,
AIC rewards a model for assigning a high probability to the data and penalises it for each
parameter that it needed to do so.

For the owls we compare the Negative Binomial model, with two parameters, with the Poisson
model, with one, whose maximum log-likelihood is calculated at its estimate, the mean of the
sample (for a model fitted with `optim()`, the maximum log-likelihood is minus the element
`value` of the fit). Only differences in AIC matter, so we also calculate the difference
between each model and the one with the lowest AIC:

```{r}
# Maximised log-likelihood, number of estimated parameters K and AIC for the two models
# fitted to the owl data. AIC = 2K - 2 * log-likelihood.
loglik_poisson = sum(dpois(x = call_counts, lambda = mu_mom, log = TRUE))
aic_table = data.frame(
  model = c("Poisson", "Negative Binomial"),
  K = c(1, 2),
  loglik = c(loglik_poisson, loglik_nb)
)
aic_table$aic = 2 * aic_table$K - 2 * aic_table$loglik

# Only differences in AIC matter: difference from the lowest value.
aic_table$delta_aic = aic_table$aic - min(aic_table$aic)
aic_table
```

The difference of 667 units in favour of the Negative Binomial model is very large
compared with the two units that its additional parameter costs, in agreement with what
@fig-owl_fits showed.

The justification of AIC is asymptotic, and when the number of observations $n$ is small
compared with the number of parameters $K$ the term $2K$ is too small to properly penalise
complex models: the criterion then tends to prefer models with too many parameters. The
**corrected AIC** (AICc) adds a penalty that is large when $n$ is close to $K$ and
disappears as $n$ grows:^[The correction was derived by Sugiura (1978) for linear regression
with Normal errors and extended by Hurvich and Tsai (1989), "Regression and time series
model selection in small samples", *Biometrika*. Burnham and Anderson (2002), *Model
selection and multimodel inference*, recommend AICc whenever $n/K$ is smaller than about
40.]

$$
\mathrm{AICc}
=\mathrm{AIC}+\frac{2K(K+1)}{n-K-1}
=2K\,\frac{n}{n-K-1}-2\,\ell(\hat\theta),
$$

where $n$ is the number of observations and $K$ and $\ell(\hat\theta)$ are the same as in
AIC. The correction needs $n>K+1$. In plain English, each parameter costs $2n/(n-K-1)$
units instead of two: slightly more than two in a moderate sample, and a lot more when the
sample has hardly more observations than parameters. AICc is used in the same way as AIC,
as a difference between models fitted to the same observations. For the owls the
additional penalty is negligible (0.03 units for the Poisson model and 0.10 for the
Negative Binomial model), because the 122 visits are many more than the one or two
parameters.

The expression above comes from linear regression with Normal errors, and for the
non-linear models with other distributions that we use in this course it is an
approximation: there is no general formula for the small-sample bias of AIC. AICc is
nevertheless common in the ecological literature, where samples are often small, and a
correction that is approximately right is better than none, so you will meet it often.

AIC ranks the candidate models that we give it. It does not tell us whether the best of
them describes the data well: the Negative Binomial model is far better than the Poisson
model for the owls, and it is still an approximation of the data generating process (for
one thing, we treated visits to the same nest as i.i.d.). [Chapter 6](../Chapter_6/Theory.qmd)
returns to model comparison with further tools (BIC, cross-validation) and with checks of
goodness of fit.

Many authors use AIC to reject models that differ largely from the best model and this may
be used as a form of hypothesis testing. That is, if adding a new term to your model does
not lower the AIC by more than two units, that new model is rejected.
This is a form of null hypothesis testing in disguise and the new term is treated as if it
was "not significant". This carries over all the issues of null hypothesis testing discussed
in [Chapter 1](../Chapter_1/Theory.qmd) and it may actually be worse. Traditional statistics
has developed several techniques to control false positive error rates (e.g. when testing
many hypotheses at the same time, as in post-hoc tests) which do not exist for AIC. Instead,
we can have a more nuanced view of model comparison, where AIC is just one of the criteria
that we use to contrast different models and in many cases there might not be a true reason
to make any choice (i.e., scientific research may not be about choices but rather about
evaluating the strength of evidence in favour of alternative hypotheses, and about making
predictions supported by evidence).

:::: {#imp-pollinator-wait .callout-important title="waiting for a pollinator"}

The waiting times between visits of pollinators to a flower are fitted with an Exponential
model, which has one parameter, and with a Gamma model, which has two. The maximum
log-likelihoods are $-231.0$ and $-230.4$. Calculate the AIC of both models. Which one has
the lower AIC? Could the log-likelihood of the Gamma model have been the lower of the two?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

For the Exponential model $\mathrm{AIC}=2\times 1+2\times 231.0=464.0$ and for the Gamma
model $\mathrm{AIC}=2\times 2+2\times 230.4=464.8$. The Exponential model has the lower
AIC, although its log-likelihood is lower: the improvement of 0.6 units of log-likelihood
does not compensate for the additional parameter. A difference of 0.8 units of AIC is very
small, so these data hardly distinguish the two models. The log-likelihood of the Gamma
model could not have been the lower one, because the Exponential distribution is a Gamma
distribution with a shape of one, and a model that contains another as a special case fits
the same data at least as well.

:::
::::

The steps of this chapter are the same for every model that we fit in the rest of the
book, so we collect them as a recipe:

::: {.callout-note title="A recipe for a fit"}
1. Write the model: the random variable, its distribution and the assumptions (for
   example, that the observations are i.i.d.).
2. Write the NLL as an R function of two lists, the parameters and the data, that starts
   with `getAll()` and uses `log = TRUE`. Transform every constrained parameter inside it
   (the logarithm for a positive parameter, the logit for a probability).
3. Connect the NLL to the data with `cmb()` and process it with `MakeADFun()`, with a
   list of starting values, for example the method-of-moments estimates.
4. Minimise the NLL with `optim()`, using the elements `par`, `fn` and `gr` of the object
   and `method = "BFGS"`, and check that `convergence` is zero.
5. Transform the estimates back to the original scale and compare the fitted model with
   the data.
6. Calculate standard errors with `sdreport()`, and Wald intervals on the scale that was
   optimised, transforming their endpoints back. For the standard error of a quantity
   calculated from the parameters, add `ADREPORT()` to the NLL.
7. Calculate likelihood profile intervals with `TMB::tmbprofile()` and `confint()` for the
   parameters that the question is about.
8. Compare the candidate models with AIC.
:::

# Summary

The likelihood is the joint probability (or density) of the observed sample, read as a
function of the parameters with the data held fixed. For i.i.d. observations it is a
product of contributions, and its logarithm, the log-likelihood, is a sum. The maximum
likelihood estimate is the parameter value with the highest likelihood. We find it by
minimising the negative log-likelihood with `optim()`, after connecting it to the data
with `cmb()` and processing it with `MakeADFun()`, because a closed-form solution
exists only for a few models. Constraints on parameters are handled with transformations
(the logarithm for positive parameters and the logit for probabilities), and invariance
allows us to transform the estimates back.

With several parameters the likelihood is a surface. Its shape depends on the
parameterisation, although the maximum and the fitted model do not. A slice fixes the
other parameters, whereas a profile re-estimates them for every value of the parameter of
interest, so the profile takes their uncertainty into account.

Uncertainty is calculated from the same likelihood. In a large sample the sampling
distribution of maximum likelihood estimators is approximately (multivariate) Normal, and
the log-likelihood near its maximum is approximately a parabola. Its curvature gives the
covariance matrix of the estimates: the more slowly the log-likelihood falls away from the
maximum, the larger the standard errors. `sdreport()` calculates the standard errors and
covariances on the scale that was optimised, and Wald intervals are calculated on that
scale and transformed back. A standard error cannot be transformed back like an estimate,
because a non-linear function does not pass through an average; the standard error of a
quantity calculated from the parameters is requested with `ADREPORT()`, which applies the
delta method, an approximation. Likelihood profile intervals,
which we calculate with `tmbprofile()`, contain the values whose profile log-likelihood is
within 1.92 units of the maximum; they do not depend on the scale and they follow the
asymmetry of the likelihood. A joint confidence region for two parameters uses a cutoff of
3.00. Simulation shows how close the coverage of each interval is to the confidence level.

Maximum likelihood estimators are consistent, asymptotically normal and asymptotically
efficient: in large samples they are centred on the parameter and no other regular
estimator is more precise. In finite samples they are in general biased, and their
sampling distribution can be far from Normal. When the model does not contain the
distribution of the data generating process (a misspecified model, @sec-misspecified), the
estimator converges to the parameter values that bring the model closest to that
process. Finally, AIC compares models fitted to the same data by penalising
the maximum log-likelihood for the number of parameters.

So far every observation had the same distribution. In
[Chapter 5](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd) we study deterministic functions that describe how an
expected response changes with a predictor, and in [Chapter 6](../Chapter_6/Theory.qmd) we
combine them with the likelihood of this chapter to fit ecological response curves.

# Chapter quiz

The questions below follow the order of the chapter. Try each question before opening its
solution.

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 1: frog egg masses"}

You count the egg masses of a frog in eight ponds and write the likelihood
$L(\lambda\mid x_1,\ldots,x_8)$ of a Poisson model. Which quantities are fixed in this
function and which one varies? Does the likelihood give the probability that $\lambda$ has
a certain value?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

The eight counts are fixed and $\lambda$ varies. The likelihood is the probability of the
observed counts for a given value of $\lambda$. It does not integrate to one over the
values of $\lambda$, and in the model $\lambda$ is a fixed quantity, so the likelihood is
not a probability distribution for $\lambda$. We use it to compare values of $\lambda$.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 2: mayfly nymphs"}

Two samples from a stream contain 2 and 0 mayfly nymphs. Assuming i.i.d. counts with a
Poisson distribution, write the likelihood as a function of $\lambda$ and evaluate it at
$\lambda=1$ and at $\lambda=2$. Which of the two values is better supported by the data?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

The likelihood is

$$
L(\lambda\mid 2,0)=\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{2}}{2!}\times e^{-\lambda}
=\frac{e^{-2\lambda}\lambda^{2}}{2}.
$$

At $\lambda=1$ it is $e^{-2}/2\approx 0.068$ and at $\lambda=2$ it is
$4e^{-4}/2\approx 0.037$. The data are better supported by $\lambda=1$, which is the mean
of the two counts.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 3: bat passes"}

A detector records the number of bat passes on each of 300 nights. Why would you calculate
the log-likelihood of a model for these counts and not the likelihood? Write an R
expression for the log-likelihood of a Poisson model with a mean of 12 passes/night,
for counts stored in a vector called `passes`.

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

The likelihood is a product of 300 probabilities, which can be smaller than the smallest
number that the computer can represent, so R may return zero. The log-likelihood is a sum
of log probabilities and does not have this problem:
`sum(dpois(x = passes, lambda = 12, log = TRUE))`.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 4: germinated seeds"}

You minimise an NLL for the mean number of germinated seeds per tray, in which the
parameter is the logarithm of the mean. `optim()` returns `par = 1.7`, `value = 96.4` and
`convergence = 0`. What is the estimate of the mean? What is the maximum log-likelihood?
What does the convergence code tell you?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

The estimate of the mean is $e^{1.7}\approx 5.5$ germinated seeds per tray. `value` is the
minimum of the NLL, so the maximum log-likelihood is $-96.4$. A convergence code of zero
means that the algorithm stopped normally.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 5: empty nest boxes"}

Under a Poisson model, the MLE of the mean number of eggs per nest box is 2.3. What is the
MLE of the probability that a nest box has no eggs? Which property of maximum likelihood
did you use?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

Under a Poisson model the probability of a count of zero is $e^{-\lambda}$. By invariance,
its MLE is $e^{-2.3}\approx 0.10$.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 6: two curves for one parameter"}

For the half-saturation parameter of a model with three parameters, the range of values
within 1.92 units of the maximum log-likelihood is 2.1 to 2.9 when the other two
parameters are fixed at their estimates, and 1.8 to 3.4 when they are re-estimated for
each value. Which of the two is a slice and which is a profile? Which would you report as
a confidence interval, and why is the other one narrower?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

The first is a slice and the second a profile. The confidence interval is the one from the
profile, 1.8 to 3.4. The slice is narrower because it treats the other two parameters as
if they were known, whereas the profile takes into account that they are estimated from
the same data.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 7: two surveys"}

Two surveys estimate the same detection probability by maximum likelihood on the logit
scale. At the maximum, the curvature of the log-likelihood (minus its second derivative) is
16 in the first survey and 64 in the second. Calculate the standard error of the estimate
on the logit scale in each survey. What does the difference in curvature say about the
data?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

The standard error is one over the square root of the curvature, so the standard errors
are $1/\sqrt{16}=0.25$ and $1/\sqrt{64}=0.125$. The log-likelihood of the second survey
is four times as sharply curved: its data discriminate better among values of
the parameter (for example, because it has four times as many observations), which halves
the standard error.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 8: seed predation"}

The relative profile log-likelihood of a seed predation rate is $-0.8$ at a rate of
0.10/day and $-2.6$ at a rate of 0.20/day. Which of these two values is inside the 95%
likelihood profile interval? Which cutoff would you use for a joint 95% confidence region
of two parameters?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

A rate of 0.10/day is inside the interval, because its relative profile log-likelihood
is above $-1.92$, and a rate of 0.20/day is outside. For a joint region of two
parameters the cutoff is half the 0.95 quantile of a chi-squared distribution with two
degrees of freedom, `qchisq(p = 0.95, df = 2) / 2`, which is approximately 3.00.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 9: parasites on fish"}

For counts of parasites per fish under a Negative Binomial model, the method of moments
and maximum likelihood give the same estimate of the mean but different estimates of the
shape $k$. How can two methods give different estimates from the same sample? Which of the
two estimators is more precise in a large sample?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

The two methods use different information. The method of moments chooses the parameters
that reproduce the mean and the variance of the sample, whereas maximum likelihood chooses
those under which all the observed counts are most probable. In a large sample the MLE is
the more precise of the two, because it is asymptotically efficient.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 10: flower visits"}

A Poisson model fitted to counts of flower visits has a maximum log-likelihood of
$-412.6$, and a Negative Binomial model fitted to the same counts has $-389.2$. Calculate
the AIC of both models. Which model is preferred? Does this tell you that the preferred
model describes the counts well?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

The Poisson model has one parameter, so $\mathrm{AIC}=2+825.2=827.2$. The Negative
Binomial model has two, so $\mathrm{AIC}=4+778.4=782.4$. The Negative Binomial model is
preferred, with an AIC that is 44.8 units lower. AIC only ranks the models that we
compare, so it does not tell us whether the better of the two describes the counts well.

:::
::::
